government could not get the situation under control. That is exactly what happened in the year 1930. I recall, sir, that when I was sitting in the corner on the other side of the chamber, when I used to ask many questions not only of the Minister of Labour but of Mr. Bennett, the minister was nearly always silent, so much so that one day I had to tell him that I thought the cat had eaten his tongue. Of course hon. members who have received a report on unemployment drafted by a member of parliament remember very well that a false picture of the situation was put by the then prime minister in the mouth of His Excellency the Governor General. This he did not only as to the speech from the throne but also as to the prorogation speeches; it was done at the beginning and the end of each session from 1930 to 1935 inclusive. These are facts. The country was not told the truth. It was impossible for us to obtain information; orders had been given by the government of the day to the service at large not to supply members of parliament with any information on unemployment. That is why it was impossible to have a true picture of the situation.
It was then considered important to have a survey of the unemployed, to know what they did before they became unemployed, what were their previous trades and occupations. That is very easy to do provided one is willing to do it. Why do it? For several reasons. In the first place, it should be done to ascertain whether the picture painted by some hon. members is true only of their own constituencies, true of large sections of the country, or true of the country as a whole. That is the first point. It is most important to know also what are the trades which have suffered most from unemployment. It is important also to know whether there is duplication of relief. If you have a classification of the unemployed, showing their trades and previous occupations and addresses, you can ascertain whether one man is receiving relief for two people or for three people, as has happened several times. But there is another reason, more important than the others; it is that unemployment on a large scale as it has existed since 1930 is an abnormal thing, and we must come together to do something to improve the conditions in this country.
If I am not to make a political speech, on the other hand I cannot ignore the fact that the man who is mostly responsible for the condition that we have now is the former leader of the Conservative party, who is a quitter and who said when he left this country that he was going home.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: On a point of order: is " quitter " a parliamentary word to apply to an ex-prime minister?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: He is no longer a member of parliament.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The word " quitter " is not in Beauchesne; and it is not applied to one who at the present time is a member of this house.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: He is a former member.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a rule of the house to the effect that no hon. member may use offensive language with respect to the members of the royal family, His Excellency the Governor General, and members of both houses. But there is a period after that; it is finished. If the former leader of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol)-I was saying " sofa "-had chosen to remain a member of parliament, I would not have used that expression. It is because he is out of this house that I can speak freely about him. I have no grudge against him, but I think of all those who suffered so much as a result of his boastful promises to end unemployment.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Your party did the same.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Our party?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Our party said it would do the very best it could, but we have no supermen in our party and that makes a difference. Perhaps my hon. friend can find some superman in his own group. I am sure they believe they are supermen, and I can see that they are very happy in that belief.
The main reason for a survey of the unemployed according to trades or occupations is to enable the government to know what can be done with regard tb the unemployed individually. Unemployment is a sort of disease and it must be treated individually. During the war some men were wounded by shrapnel or bullets and others were gassed. Each one had to receive a particular treatment ; each had to be looked after in a separate individual way. The same should be done with unemployment. Each case should be considered individually. We should have the story of each of the unemployed to see what can be done for him and whether he is really unemployed through no fault of his own. Of course, there are many classes of unemployed persons. There are those who are unemployable. A man may be unemployable for several reasons. He may be sick and incapable of doing any work, or he may be
3010	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
unwilling to work. The first man deserves consideration, the second deserves none. On the other hand there are the fellows who are willing and able to work, and they should be helped. But they cannot be helped solely by this government; they must be helped by everyone in the country who wishes to be a good Samaritan and help his neighbour. If he wants real help he must not be given scrip, because it is not accepted in payment.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Would he work for nothing?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No, just a minute. My hon. friend is a great heckler, but I would ask him to be just as quiet when I am speaking as I am when he speaks. I do not think I have interrupted him once. I do not always listen to him, I confess. I am here in the house and when he speaks I do not always pay attention to what he says, but I leave him alone and I want him to leave me alone. If he does not like what I say he can speak afterwards.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: You don't want to learn; you forget nothing and you learn nothing.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: It is delightful to see the degree of self-satisfaction in the group to your ultimate left, Mr. Speaker. Of course, they are very nice fellows, but they remind me of the old watchmaker who once repaired a watch and forgot to put back two little wheels. It went just the same, but it did not keep time.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: It was not wasting time, either.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Were they the balance
wheels?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
When I was interrupted by one of our genial colleagues I was about to say that it is pretty difficult for the government to know exactly what to do for the unemployed unless they know what the unemployed can do; and they cannot get that knowledge except from a survey covering each individual case. I remember that in the good times of prosperity

I mean when the other government was in power-we were told that information could be secured only from the bureau of statistics. The bureau of statistics had the census figures of 1931, some years before, and it was impossible to get any accurate information. Mayors came to Ottawa and information was asked for and they said they had it. The mayor of London, Ontario, said he had it; Mr. Trepanier, an alderman of Montreal, also said he had it, but in fact neither had it. They had none at all, but they started to get the information at the request of a member of parliament, and 
Mayor Houde, the present mayor of Montreal, instructed General Panet, the head of relief in Montreal, to carry out a survey. With nine other persons he spent three weeks making a survey of the unemployed on relief, heads of families, to find out what their previous occupations had been. It was a most interesting survey. We knew what artisans were unemployed in Montreal. Of course there were many who were designated as day labourers, but there was a considerable number of men belonging to the building trade, carpenters, masons, plumbers and so on. These people could have got some help through the building industry. If we had such a survey of the unemployed as was suggested yesterday by a member of the Conservative party, we would know exactly what the situation was and the government would know what could be done to relieve unemployment in particular areas, in bad sections of the country-and when I say bad sections I mean sections where unemployment is worst.
This could easily be done by Ottawa and by the provinces through the municipalities. The municipal authorities are there on the spot. Everyone is known in the municipality, and it would be very easy for such a survey to be made. How could the dominion government get that information? WTe may be told that there is a constitutional issue in the matter, but it could very well be done by the dominion government notifying the provincial governments that they would pay nothing for relief or assistance until they got that information accurately from the municipalities through the provinces.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: They have already had it.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No. I defy my hon. friend to get that information by trades, in the cities, either from the Department of Labour or from the provincial governments. A survey was made in 1934, by Mr. Croll, who was then minister of welfare in Ontario, and to my knowledge none has been made since in any other province. The information that members get from the Department of Labour- and the minister cannot contradict me on this point-is only as to the number of those who receive relief. We have no information regarding the number of unemployed in the building industry in each municipality.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Whose fault is it that you have not that information?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is because nobody cares to get it. If members of parliament would unite in asking for that information from the

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
Department of Labour, I am sure that the minister, who is an able man, would take steps to get it for us.
I have heard some hon. members praise the employment commission, and at the beginning of the session I was even blamed for having thrown the report of that commission on the floor last year. Well, when the commission was appointed the Minister of Labour told a member of parliament that its report on unemployment, showing the previous occupations of the unemployed, was to be the basis of the policy of the government in dealing with this problem. Then that commission did absolutely nothing; its report was absolutely useless. In the first place we must have order, and to get order we must have a real insight into the situation. We must know what is going on; we must know what places throughout the country are suffering from unemployment; we must know the trades in which there are the most unemployed, in order that we may do something to relieve that condition.
Now let me tell the minister for his own benefit, and for the benefit of the government and of the country at large, that I am very suspicious as to the competence of some of his assistants. I fear that in the Department of Labour there are some men who were appointed by the previous administration who are not competent to handl: their jobs. In my humble view the minister should be closer and closer to members of parliament in discussing this question of unemployment. He means well; he is an able man, and that is what should be done. He should be very careful about what is said by those immediately under him, who are not in the least competent to deal with such a great problem as unemployment. We must consider things differently when we have such a huge problem to deal with than in ordinary times, when life is easy and nothing out of the ordinary is going on.
What should be done for the relief of unemployment? In the maritimes they_ want help for the fishermen and something in the way of defence works. The same applies to British Columbia. Why does not the government give them defence works and help the fishermen? In the province of Quebec they want public works for the relief of unemployment. Let us have public works in that province. In the west they clamour for assistance to the farmers. In Ontario they want expenditures on defence works. Give the people what they want, as long as it is reasonable, to make them happy and comfortable. That is my understanding of the
situation. But do not give them what they do not ask for; let them ask for something before giving it to them.
Many very useful things could be done to-day. I regret very much that any man who is fit should have to live on relief, on a small amount that barely keeps him from starvation. He should have enough on which to live decently. A friend of mine in the Antipodes, an old member of parliament in Australia, sent me the report of a speech he made in Canberra advocating the free distribution of milk to school children in order to give them the food they need to keep them healthy. We could do many things like that; I need not enumerate them all. This is a kind of social welfare that could be carried on by any government, or by the federal government in conjunction with the provincial governments. But it is impossible to believe that we can go forward one step in dealing with the question of unemployment unless we try to establish order in this country; not military order but order under which every man will be where he belongs. Many men who were good tradesmen before they became unemployed are not so good now. They feel rusty; they cannot work so easily or so well as before, and men of this kind, if they were technicians, should have easier jobs than those they formerly held.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) made some good suggestions and some others not so good. He deserves credit for making recommendations. He worked pretty hard to prepare his oration, and it is too bad that he went too far and made one statement that was a grease spot on his speech. I was not surprised, sir, that he was called upon to withdraw what he said. He made a statement, which statement was denied, and according to parliamentary practice the only thing for him to do is bring in evidence in rebuttal to show that those who denied what he said were wrong and that he was right. Unless he does that at some future time people will be very suspicious as to the reliability of his information. On the other hand we must not deal with unemployment in a too scientific way. Marshal Foch, victor in the great war, used to say that warfare was common sense. The warfare against unemployment should be common sense also. I regret very much that my good friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) should have declared that this government had done absolutely nothing for unemployment.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
That is some progress.
Perhaps if I asked the hon, gentleman another question he would say this government had done very well. But since my hon. friend is in his seat and not in the witness box I will not pursue my questioning.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that my remarks have been made in a very friendly spirit. I hope that when we discuss unemployment hon. members will not practise extravagance and picture things as worse than they really are. It will be good for the house and the country to learn the bare truth about the situation. In addition I will ask the Minister of Labour, for his own good, for the good of the government and the country, to scrutinize what has been done by some officials of his department in regard to the relief of unemployment. He will find that it is nil. I do not put the blame on him; I think it only fair to make that distinction, but in these times we need the very best men if we are to settle those most difficult problems. It is not a question of sympathy. I have sympathy for every human soul, but when I see a man enjoying a fine and lucrative position at the expense of hundreds of thousands of others, who suffer from his incompetency, I say to the minister: If you are not soft-hearted, throw him out and protect the other thousands.
Some hon. members will of course say that some civil servants or officials are not in the house. Of course they are not. But each civil servant is represented by his minister; his minister has to speak for him. So that the minister may better understand what I have said, I would point out that I have no grudge against anybody, but I want the Department of Labour to be a real department of labour, to be effective, to help the people, and to be worthy of the minister and of the government. Therefore I will not insist upon it; but instead of showing sympathy to one or two or three or four individuals, show sympathy to the big crowd, and the people will understand you and appreciate you, and will be with you.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): Mr. Speaker, we are not yet in committee but-

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I would draw the attention of the minister to the fact that if he speaks he will close the debate.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
On the question raised by the previous speaker (Mr. Pouliot), which I think might properly be regarded as a question of privilege, I do feel that I ought immediately to make a reply. He has made reference to those in the Department of (Mr. ManionJ
Labour charged immediately with the administration of unemployment relief. He is entirely entitled to his opinion, and I take it to express that opinion in the house, but I would like to say to him that in my experience in the Department of Labour, and speaking as generally as he has done, I have found the officials of that department, regardless of whether or not they were there before I took office, most loyal, most industrious and most faithful in the discharge of their duties.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not take more than five or six minutes. In this long debate I believe we have heard every reason for the condition known as unemployment, but only from this corner of the house has there been mention of the financial system.
Hon. members in this group are blamed for bringing up the subject of money on every possible occasion. But, if I may say so, when one comes to see the light of truth one realizes it is impossible to study almost any subject without looking at it from the point of view of finance and money.
If I might digress for a moment, I happen to have a passion for classical music. During the last session the commentator for one of the great symphonic orchestras of the United States invited his radio listeners to send in their comments respecting a comparison between old classical music and modern serious music. During the Easter recess last year, having a little time on my hands, I sent in my ideas respecting modern music, and I said in part that whatever might be said of the merits of modern serious music it would have to be admitted that it was becoming more and more pessimistic. I traced, in a way which I shall not now go into, the tendency towards pessimism in music, to the rise of "the money power."

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Right after the birth of social credit.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I notice that produces a smile on the faces of some hon. members. However, the Sunday on which the commentator would have read my communication happened to coincide with the Sunday when the honorary secretary of the orchestra, the wife of one of the great financiers in the United States, was making an appeal to the radio audience for subscriptions for the orchestra. That being so, I believe the commentator decided to rule my communication out of order-anyway he did not read it. But he did send me a note in these words, "I agree entirely with your views on modern music. And why ? This particular com-

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
mentator is a very distinguished composer of music. When we consider the disastrous effect that the rising power of money has had on the composers of music, perhaps we can understand the disastrous effect money power has had on the mind of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), and why his economic compositions become more and more pessimistic.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
suggest that the Department of Labour should employ an orchestra?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I am merely suggesting that this money power or, if you like, the rule of money, in every walk of life, has had a most paralyzing and disastrous effect on the human mind.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: AVe are not in that class.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Then, if I may descend
from the sublime to the ridiculous, may I say that people were wont, as the saying goes, to enjoy themselves with wine, women and song-now, I believe, the expression is gin, jazz, sugar daddies and hot mammas.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: And peanut butter.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Would this be a fair statement of the Liberal or, if you like, the orthodox viewpoint of the question we have been discussing. Number one, that the unemployed, or the victims, have no real claim on the state; number two, that there is nothing wrong with the monetary system itself and that unemployment is not due to maladjustments or fundamental flaws in the financial system, and, number three, that the only remedy is the one set out the night before last by the minister, namely the expansion of foreign trade.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: One remedy.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I think that is a fair statement, and I hope I am not regarded as being in any way politically biased, because I used to support one of the old-line parties. I have in my hand a book from which I should like to read one paragraph. It is headed "Monetary policy of plenty instead of scarcity", and contains the hearings before the committee on banking and currency of the house of representatives of the United States. The, opinions which I am about to read-

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Who is the author?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
This is a copy of the
evidence given before the committee on banking and currency of the house of representatives when it was considering a monetary policy of plenty instead of scarcity.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Who gave the evidence?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Perhaps I had better read it.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I am sorry I asked for it.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
This committee corresponds to our own committee on banking and commerce and is made up largely of men with the same upbringing and surroundings as the members of our committee. I suppose this committee represents the best financial thought in possibly the greatest nation in the world, certainly the richest in industry and production. I have no reason to believe that any of the members of this committee are called social crediters, but apparently they have come to see the light. The first point they deal with is whether the victims of unemployment have any claim upon the state, and they say this:
The more highly a people are civilized, the more often its genius is demonstrated in the work of an individual. Genius is not altogether the result of the merit of the individual, but of the society from which it springs, and the higher the society, the higher the social organization, the more often that genius demonstrates itself.
The one that makes the demonstration should, of course, receive, to a very considerable extent, the results of whatever he has been able to do. Unfortunately, an inventor is very often not the one who receives the benefit of the invention. Nevertheless, it is just that he should. But in the last analysis the society from which he springs is entitled-and all of that society- to the benefit of what he invents. And not he and not a small group that may have had the business acumen to grab the invention and make use of it. The society which has made possible that genius is entitled ultimately to its benefits.
I think that statement justifies what we in this corner of the house have said. The next paragraph, which deals with the bearing of finance upon employment, reads:
Here we have a condition under our present monetary and industrial system in which we concede that we are not able to consume all of the wanted goods and services that we are able to produce. AVe concede that, all of us- every member of this committee concedes that.
Every member of that committee on banking and currency of the United States congress concedes what we in this corner have been saying over and over again, and 'been laughed at for saying. Every member of that committee conceded that it is impossible for an industrialized nation to consume what it produces. The report continues:
All right: AVe all work in an endeavour to consume that part of production which is possible. Then we undertake to put in operation a law which will enable us to consume the balance of it. Is there anything immoral about that? Is there anything that smacks of getting something for nothing about that? Is it better
3014	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
that we should receive what we can produce rather than produce and dump it over into Europe or Asia or some other place? Which is wiser? Which is more just? To produce it for ourselves or to produce it to give it away- and it does not make any difference whether we give it away by the dumping process or whether we give it away by a process of loaning money to the foreign countries which they are to respend in this country, and which debts will never be paid? And that is what has been going on in this country for years and years and years.
That represents the opinion of the committee on banking and currency of the United States congress, and I think it is identical with what we in this group here have so often put before this house.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), I found I was able to agree with him on one point, but I had to disagree with him on another. I agreed with him when he concluded by saying that since the present government came into office the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) had done nothing to diminish unemployment. That is why I rise now to say something on this bill, which is similar to the bills we have had presented every session since 1931. I disagreed with the hon. member for Temiscouata when he said in his opening remarks that we had no unemployment until the Conservative party brought it about in 1930, or words to that effect.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Do you agree with the hon. member on that?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No, I do not agree with him on that.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: You are right on that.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
We'had serious unemployment long before the depression which began in the fall of 1929. Those who, both politically and economically, spoke for the working class, were advocating means of alleviating the effect of unemployment years before this depression set in. I have in my hand a statement submitted by the executive of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada to the forty-seventh annual convention of that organization, held in Vancouver in September, 1931. This statement contains a review of the policies of the congress on employment, unemployment and under-employment from 1883, when the congress was organized, to 1931 and points out that from its inception the congress had been confronted with the question of unemployment. We find the congress discussing 
unemployment at its first convention held in 1883, and moving for a reduction in the hours of labour to nine hours a day on the grounds:
That the labour market is at present glutted, and if the resolution is adopted it will result in giving work to many who are out of it to-day as employers would find it necessary to employ more men.
Three years later we find the congress again discussing unemployment at its annual convention and passing a resolution asking the government to enact a bill to regulate the hours of labour of workers in the employ of the government.
In 1895 unemployment was again rife, and of course in between these periods we had unemployment too, but those were the high points of unemployment as we come down through the years and the cycle of prosperity recedes and bad times return.
The new west was being opened up about that time, and the trades congress executive put forward land settlement as a relief measure. It is interesting at this point to note how rapidly we have moved in the last fifty years. In 1895 the four western provinces were practically undeveloped, but within a little less than fifty years we have watched these new provinces being opened up and developed. We have seen enormous wealth extracted from their resources. Now we are witnessing their economic decline. This, it seems to me, should make us pause, to realize that we are no longer in the world of fifty or thirty or even twenty years ago.
Two years later, in 1897, the unemployment situation was still bad, and the congress advocated the restriction of immigration and the establishment of free employment bureaux, both of which were done.
In 1914 unemployment had again reached alarming proportions, and at the congress that year we find representatives of the trades unions asking the government to give the same treatment to labour as it was then by legislation giving to capital. The trades and labour congress of 1914 adopted a resolution urging the federal government to convene a conference of provincial and municipal authorities, boards of trade and labour councils to -formulate measures for dealing with the widespread unemployment and destitution then prevailing throughout the dominion. I understand that a similar conference was proposed this afternoon, and I believe it was proposed a few days ago by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion). But the suggestion is not new.
For a few years during the war we did not hear much about unemployment. The people

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
of the great nations of the world, and we along with them, were so busy fighting each other and manufacturing the instruments of death and destruction that there was work for almost everyone. But with the end of the war again came unemployment. I presume that when the dove of peace brought the olive branch, it also brought with it the spectre of unemployment.
In 1921 the trades congress urged the adoption of unemployment insurance, or as they called it, state employment insurance.
Then for a few years we had prosperity, in 1925, 1926, 1927, 1928 and up to the fall of 1929. But as the Minister of Labour pointed out when speaking, I believe, on the address, we had considerable unemployment even in those days. The estimated figure for unemployment which the minister gave for January, 1930, was 297,000, but I submit that there is a vast difference between 300,000 unemployed in 1930 and the years before, and 300,000 unemployed since 1930. In the years before the depression the unemployed were out of work for only short periods, and they had reserves to carry them over these periods, but, as I shall point out later, the unemployment of to-day is largely unemployment that is continuous.
I am firmly of the opinion that without a drastic change in our economy we are not likely to have a smaller number of unemployed at any time than we have at present, and we may as well make up our minds that the period of expansion which we have known on this continent for the last hundred years is definitely over. That period of expansion was able to take care not only of the ordinary supply of labour and its normal increase, but of millions more who came to this continent from the older countries of Europe, and some from Asia as well.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
That is, certainly, an
extremely pessimistic view.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It may appear to be a pessimistic view, but it need not be because we were never better able to supply the needs of our people than we are to-day. We have the natural resources; we have the capital and equipment; we have the intelligence and ability to manage these things, and to develop our resources on a greater scale than ever before. Surely under such conditions there is no need for pessimism. If. that is the case, and I maintain that it is, no time should be lost in setting our economic house in order, so as to put a stop to the mental, physical and moral decay which is gradually sapping the vitality not only of our unemployed but of our people as a whole.
At the beginning of the depression the people who were unemployed-not ali of them, but a great proportion of them-had reserves, and those reserves were not all material. Some were material and some were psychological. They had homes, many of which were paid for; they had equities in homes, and hoped some day to be able to own them outright; they had reserves of clothes, furniture and other household goods. But all those reserves are now depleted. In addition, they had reserves of hope, courage and inspiration-spiritual reserves which are now as much depleted as are their material reserves.
A great many of the unemployed were broken in spirit before they went on relief. Most went on relief reluctantly. To make matters worse, as I pointed out in the house the other day, when they do get employment for short periods and go off relief they have to go through the most humiliating experiences before they are able to get back on the relief rolls again. This continual investigating so affects sensitive persons that they refuse short periods of work. The unemployed should, in my opinion, always be regarded as human beings with feelings like our own. They should be encouraged to accept whatever work is offered, and be allowed to use earnings from employment for brief periods without being too closely investigated as to what they do with such earnings.
In any steps taken to rehabilitate the unemployed we must keep in mind that spiritual rehabilitation is even more necessary than the satisfying of physical needs. That is, the unemployed must be made to feel that they are an essential part of society, that they are useful in the scheme of things. That can be done only if they feel that the work they are doing is useful and that they have a share in directing it. Indeed, even without unemployment, the present industrial system dehumanizes the manual worker.
Last fall I was able to spend a few weeks in the maritime provinces and investigate some of the work which has been done there during the last eight or nine years by the cooperative movement. What appeared to me most important was not the economic effects upon the people, not the financial rewards which it brought them, but its psychological effect in bringing back the self-respect of poverty-stricken people. I feel convinced that until such time as we can place our people in a position where they feel they have a stake in the country, it is futile to expect cooperation from them in building up our society, or in playing an important part, or in giving all that they can give in the building of a good

society. I would impress that upon the minister, who is, I believe, interested in that phase of this important question. What we must realize to-day is that our economy is trying to adjust itself to a diminishing demand. Industrial institutions are becoming geared to a stable production and consequently to a more or less stable labour personnel. The unemployed of to-day are, as I said a moment ago, in large part those who were unemployed five or six years ago. In this connection I should like to quote a statement made recently by Doctor R. H. Coats, dominion statistician, who is this year president of the American Statistical Association. He made the statement it the annual meeting of that body, which took place in Detroit. As reported in the Vinnipeg Free Press, he said:
The problem is not that all or most workers are sometimes employed and sometimes not, but a differentiation which is hardening into two classes-the seldom unemployed and the seldom employed.
I would ask hon. members to listen to this. This statement was not made by a politician or a man who is interested in what the public thinks of what he says.

speechtext: Would it have been less true if it had been made by some person who is a politician?

Thus the unemployed are, first, a sort of human scaffolding set aside when an expanding stage in enterprise is over; second, a series of discards as enterprise works out its operating requirements. *
I am a socialist, and many years ago my reading and study of economics led me to realize that the worker in industry is, so far as his employer is concerned, merely a ' factor in industry in the same way as the raw material, the machinery and the other elements which make up the product. If any proof is required of that, I consider the evidence of this government official is of value.

We must admit that this statement by Doctor Coats is true. But if we accept the truth of it, what are we going to do about it? It is of the nature of discards to deteriorate quickly, and human discards are no exception. If you are going to maintain the morale of the people you must keep those people continually in an environment which builds morale rather than destroys it. The moment people feel that they are discards, mere human scaffolding which has been set aside when the job has been finished, there begins a deterioration of the spiritual values which are necessary if we are to build an orderly human society. This country cannot afford to have a part of its population in the position of being mere factors in production, mere human scaffolding to be set aside when a certain process is finished. Nor can this country afford to have numbers of its people thrown on the scrap-heap as refuse once they have fulfilled the social need of the moment. If we attempt to do that our civilization will go the way of every civilization built on slave labour.
Last evening I read a statement which was made in this chamber by the Minister of Labour. I had read it, but before I reached the point of elaborating on it I was asked a question by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), and in answering it_ I forgot to comment on the statement. I wish to read that statement again and comment on it briefly. It was made in answer to the following question by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou) at page 3165:

The minister replied:
Mr. Chairman, I am bound to say the hon. member has put a difficult question. I say that frankly to him. I did believe three years ago there was a reasonable prospect, given a return to normal conditions of international trade, that this country could absorb from year to year the annual accretion of potential wage-earners. Lacking normal conditions of trade, it lias not been possible for this country to do that thing.

If we take any particular period, say, the period from 1925, when we had relatively prosperous times, to 1929, when the collapse came, the question arises, what caused the break-down then? You could not blame that situation on disturbed world conditions such as exist to-day;

I have listened in the last few days, in fact in the last few years, to discussions on unemployment and solutions put forward for overcoming the problem; and as far as I can learn, the Liberal party, the government of the day, maintains that unemployment can be ended or lessened only by a great increase in foreign trade. What I want to point out is that there is one respect in which these three parties agree. it means leaving the planning and control of industries in the hands of individuals, and that means leaving the livelihood of the people in the control of private monopoly. I need only refer to the price spreads and mass buying commission of 1934-35, and the Turgeon commission of 1936. Both these investigations prove my contention.
The group to which I belong, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, believes on the other hand, that unemployment and the problems associated with it are caused fundamentally by the profit economy itself. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) pointed out, unemployment has evolved from the economic system; but this does not mean that the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) was right when he said that we want the state to put everyone to work and to regulate every

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was pointing out that to-day private industry had _ become private monopoly, that it was exploiting the people of the country. I should like to put on record in that regard the words of one who, I think, will be considered, at least by a large number of the members of this house, as a greater authority than I. I quote from Hansard for February 27, 1933, at page 2510. The speaker was the present right, hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). He on that occasion outlined the policy of the Liberal party on which they were returned to power in 1935. Referring to production and distribution, this in part is what he had to say:
The system of distribution of products needs overhauling. Distribution should be on a service at cost basis. The spread in prices is too great, as any comparison of prices paid to producers with prices consumers have to pay will make self evident.
For years we have been harping on that very fact, without any effect to date. Further on, during the same speech, the Prime Minister said:
Industry has been adversely affected by the control exercised over industry, not by industrial managers so much as by promoters and financiers. We believe the interlocking of directorates is one of the factors which on the one hand enables bankers to control industries, and on the other hand enables industrialists to control the banks. It is our. view that in that connection there is room for much in the way of reform.
That was said over six years ago, yet I submit that the present government has not taken one step to bring about those reforms. All we have is this same old bill to which hon. members opposite were objecting in 1935 and 1933.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yes_ This in fact is what we in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group have been saying for years. We have been saying that to-day industry, instead of being used to supply the needs of the people, is used to exploit the people. Without using the term "exploitation," the Prime Minister made it abundantly clear that
(Mr. Maclnnis.l
to-day the people are being exploited by the financiers and the industrialists, who are in fact the same people. That is a fact which, if I may say so in all kindliness, our Social Credit friends evidently cannot realize. I say "evidently cannot realize" because I am sure they are seeking for a way out of this difficulty just as earnestly as any of us.
Not only is production being curtailed today in the interests of profit making. In increasing measure private capital is refusing to do what we have been told so often was the only .justification for the toll it levied on the community; that is, it refuses to take the risks incidental to the investment of new capital or capital of any kind. In that regard I should like to quote very briefly from Canadian Business, which, I believe, is the official organ of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I am quoting from the issue of February, 1939, from an article reviewing economic prospects in Canada, the United States and Great Britain:
Following a 25 per cent improvement in American business during the last six months of 1938, a levelling-off is now being experienced. At the moment there is nothing to indicate anything more than a moderate curtailment in industrial production. There is nothing serious to liquidate. Securities are in strong hands; inventories are more or less normal; there is no over-expansion in industry; there has been no building boom. The sore spot is government spending.
From 1933 to 1937, the United States government spent its way to recovery. Consumption followed this spending. And private investment in capital goods followed on the heels of consumption. In 1937, there was an apparent amount of deficit spending on the part of Washington but a closer examination of the accounts show that, including social security taxes, the government balanced its books.
And note this:
This abrupt cheek in deficit Bpending affected consumption. As consumption was reduced, new private investment was at once postponed, and the stock markets went into a tail spin. In 1938, public spending was resumed and up went consumption and the stock market. But there has been virtually no resumption of new financing. Consequently, if government spending is to slacken its momentum, the effect on business might be immediate and sharp.
So that to-day private capital refuses to take chances and industry can be kept going only by government spending. And these same capitalists who will not invest their own capital object to government spending. I have just one more short quotation from page 18 of the March issue of the same magazine, from an article by S. C. Scobell, and this reference is to Canada:
Early in 1937, our favourable balance of trade was beginning to contract. This tended to squeeze us a little. The winter slump in the

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
mining market checked the flow of new money into this industry. At the same time, the government started to balance its books in a most admirable fashion. Business was pleased, inventories were accumulated, but gradually consumption started to contract as government deficit spending on this continent virtually disappeared. New private investment-which had never acquired bold long term vision-was postponed. Savings remained idle and throughout most of 1938 Canadian business dragged listlessly. Of course, external influences have exerted a tremendous influence on our economy, but the failure of business to carry on in late 1936 and early 1937, when Ottawa stopped its deficit spending, and its failure to develop new investment outlets was partially responsible for the poor showing of our business index during 1938.
On March 15 the minister staked his hope of recovery on the expectation that private industry, private capital, would begin again to invest in new enterprises. But that, I submit, cannot be done to-day; first, because the field of investment is limited and is becoming increasingly so, and second, because the insecurity of private investment is also increasing daily.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon on the second reading of this bill it was suggested by the Speaker that I should reply when the bill was in committee to two questions which had been put to me, and I think I can do that now on this section 3. The hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght)-I thought he was present in the chamber-put a question to me to which I was not permitted to give a complete answer. I was not imputing motives to the premier of Ontario or the premier of Quebec, but I had understood that each of these gentlemen at some time recently declared that the responsibility for the solution of these social problems, which we were discussing this afternoon, and for the appropriation of the money which will be required for the solution of these problems, was the sole responsibility of the dominion parliament and the dominion government. Associated with those declarations were further pronouncements, as I understood, that they as the premiers of those two provinces were not in favour of any amendment to the British North America Act which would make it clear that this parliament might lawfully appropriate moneys for those purposes.
I was merely suggesting this afternoon that [DOT] a decision should be obtained from the highest judicial authority as to the responsibility of the dominion parliament and the dominion government, and as to whether the revenues in the dominion consolidated fund might lawfully be appropriated for those purposes. If a decision were given that it was not lawful to make such appropriations, I have confidence in the two premiers to whom I have referred sufficient to believe that each of them would thereupon agree to such amendments to the British North America Act as would clearly authorize the parliament of Canada to make such appropriations and clearly authorize the dominion government to administer such appropriations for the purposes to which they were to be applied. But, before we can come to an agreement with the several provinces or reach a sound basis of negotiation, it seems to me necessary, and expedient as well, that a judicial determination should be obtained as to what our duties and responsibilities are, and as to what extent we may make appropriations of dominion funds for those purposes.
I wish also to make a remark to my hon. friend the member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson), and to say that I can see no inconsistency ^ whatever in the position I have taken through' out a long number of years with regard to the authority of the federal parliament. I gave this afternoon certain suggested inferences from a very recent decision of the judicial

committee. Whether I was drawing proper inferences and the same inferences which the judicial committee itself would draw depends upon a further discussion of this question before the supreme court and the judicial committee, and that is all I am suggesting.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), who, I regret, is not now present, also made a strong presentation of the humanitarian point of view. I shall not take any exception to what he said because I have not the facts before me which would enable me to do so, and therefore I presume that the quotations which he made are a correct statement of the actual facts. But the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is intolerant of any suggestion in favour of procuring judicial interpretations of the British North America Act. To him I say that we are not free, under a federal system, to make appropriations for all purposes. Our legislative authority is circumscribed by the terms of the British North America Act, and therefore in order that we may act conscientiously, seriously, and may I add, honestly, in the discharge of our duties, it is necessary that we should from time to time be instructed by judicial authority as to the extent of our legislative and administrative powers.
I confess that while I have great sympathy with suffering, and especially the suffering of those who are not employed, I still cannot sympathize to the full with the attitude which the hon. member took this afternoon. The veiy fact that people are in necessitous circumstances, suffering and in need of assistance, does not justify a man taking money from the first treasury upon which he can lay his hands in order to remedy the evil and provide relief for such suffering. I remember seeing the other day a plea made by an official of a prominent bank who had misappropriated and expended some thousands of dollars, to the effect that his family were in need, his wife and family were sick and required medical care, and so he had appropriated-the court said "misappropriated"-some of the funds of the bank under his care for the purpose of providing medical attendance and care for his wife and family.
The situation is pretty nearly the same if we make appropriations of public funds of which we are trustees for purposes which we know to be invalid and illegal. There is a doubt as to the validity of these appropriations; everyone will admit that. But we are going on, and I have no objection to going on temporarily, making and administering these [DOT] appropriations. But I do say that as members of this parliament performing a public trust it is our duty and responsibility to see

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
that these doubts are removed and settled by the highest judicial authority possible. If that judicial authority in its final judgment shall decide that the appropriations which we have made and are now making are invalid and illegal, then we should take the position that we shall cease making them unless the governments of the several provinces will agree with us to modify the terms of the British North America Act to such an extent, at least, as will enable us to make such appropriations valid and legal for the future.
One other remark I would have made to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre if he were present, and that is that in discussing this act on the second reading I was not dealing with permanent relief. If he had taken the trouble to read this bill he would have seen that the appropriations which are being made for relief expire on March 31, 1940. They extend for one year only. It is true that in another section of the bill there are certain provisions for renewals of loans and advances already made but extending beyond March 31, 1940. But in respect of the relief for the indigent and the unemployed, that seotion expires, if I read the terms correctly, on March 31, 1940. So that we are here dealing only temporarily with the subject matter which I was discussing; and my contention was that, certainly within the year if possible, before this relief measure expires and before the government should come to parliament with another relief measure, the necessary procedure ought to be taken for a reference to the supreme court and to the judicial committee to ascertain exactly where we are and what we may do in a valid and legal manner.
Such a final decision from the judicial committee would enable the government and parliament to deal with embarrassing questions as to the validity of the appropriations which we are now making, and also enable the government to place before the premiers of the several provinces the fact that, in view of the decision of the judicial committee, which would then be finally obtained, it is necessary to have the consent of the provincial governments to such modifications of the British North America Act as will render such appropriations valid and legal. I am not making any partisan presentation of the case; I am simply dealing with a matter which, if studied, will prove embarrassing to most hon. members when they are brought face to face with the agitation which is being carried on from the Atlantic to the Pacific, to the effect that it is the sole duty and responsibility of the government and parliament of Canada to make the appropriations 71492-191
for relief which all citizens regard as necessary. I am not discussing the extent of relief; that is a matter for consideration each year; but I am dealing with the fact that these doubts should be allayed before parliament and especially before the electors can give a serious and conscientious decision upon the issues which have been placed before them.

speechtext:
This bill must be judged in the light of experience. We have had experience for three or four years of the working of the provisions contained in this measure. The bill has been weighed in the balance and has been found wanting, and it is among those things that have been condemned in briefs which have been submitted to the Rowell commission. The minister apparently is going to postpone, until the receipt of that commission's report, any measure of active relief for the unemployed, from the point of view of unemployment insurance, but he is willing to perpetuate the mistakes that have already been made. These mistakes have been fatal to the principles of section 3 of this bill.
In the first place, according to decisions handed down in the courts, this parliament has jurisdiction only, first, if an emergency exists and, second, if what is undertaken is for the general advantage of Canada. The minister smiles, -but that is correct. His predecessor, Mr. Heenan, stated as Minister of Labour that this parliament had nothing to do with unemployment. He said that unemployment was a matter for the provinces and municipalities. Well, that was all changed by the introduction of relief under this bill. The old state of affairs has been altered. Under the former administration agreements were made direct with the larger municipalities. In the municipalities of Ontario and of Quebec we find the people who are paying eighty-five per cent of the taxes collected by the dominion. This money goes into the consolidated revenue fund and is derived from various sources, including sales tax and income tax, and these large municipalities, under this bill, must deal with the provinces.
71492-19X4
For the last three years I have been moving for a return under section 3 of these unemployment relief measures, and the papers brought down have disclosed some interesting facts. I am not quarrelling with anything done for Montreal, which is an industrial city from which a good deal of revenue is obtained. But what has Montreal been given? Municipal and local works of all kinds-macadam roads, parks, botanical gardens, schools, hospitals, roadways and driveways; and we find that Three Rivers has been given a courthouse and other municipal institutions-because the province of Quebec is friendly to the government. But in Ontario did we get any such hand-outs? No. The minister smiles, and he is from Ontario.
Yesterday, in paying a tribute to him, I admitted that his position was a- difficult, tiresome and thankless one. It nearly killed two members of our party, his predecessors, in this house. I should like to take some of the heavy burden off the minister and his officials, and I recommend that he look into the Couzens report in the United States. What was their policy? They appointed Mr. Hopkins, who has the handling of relief for 127,000,000 people, and under his policy there is a standard plan which, if applied to Canada, would require that Hamilton, for example, in order to get any municipal institutions should conform to certain standard federal plans and conditions laid down to qualify for any work. They would have to say whether the money was to come out of income or capital; they would have to indicate the term of the bonds, whether the work was in the public interest, what the municipal debt was, the necessity of the work, the labour provided, and so on. In my opinion, as I said yesterday, the policy of this government under this bill is simply a Santa Claus handout policy. They are handing out benefits just as Santa Claus hands out presents at Christmas. I have just referred to the courthouse at Three Rivers and I am glad the people there got it. But when we ask for similar favours in Ontario we cannot get them or hardly anything. There may be a little difference of opinion between the province of Ontario and the dominion, and for that reason the governor in council declines to make any recommendation under section 3; or if he does make a recommendation, the province of Ontario will not recommend these local works and so we get nothing.
There are some other objections to the bill. It is not in the public interest that we should continue the present system which, I repeat, has been weighed in the balance and found wanting. In the first place the bill

does not create employment, nor is there any standard plan or any estimate of the cost. We have simply an agreement between this parliament and certain favoured provinces, and those provinces get all the plums at the expense of others. The government is just a Santa Claus handing out presents. Why, the city of Ottawa receives consideration under this bill and some six or seven acts and agreements. Other places should get equality of treatment. It gets votes which no other municipality can get. I have found about six agreements under which Ottawa obtains assistance. I am not objecting to that, but I want to see the same way of helping other places.
The explanatory note declares that this bill is in the same form as the act of 1938, with the addition of assistance in respect to youth training, and section 3 provides that the governor in council may, out of moneys appropriated by parliament, authorize the execution of such undertakings as the governor in council may determine.
In the return I received there were nearly 1,600 different items, and I found that Ontario was getting very little if anything under this or any other act. Ontario does not even come under the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, because the government at Queens Park say they will not have anything to do with that sort of thing except some roads of their own. It seems to me the principle of section 3 is this by provinces: To him that hath shall be given and from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath. That is the principle of the whole legislation. The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) is on the good roads commission of York township; I want him to listen to this discussion, because he should not be asking the city of Toronto or the province of Ontario to hand out money for good roads there when he can come here to Ottawa like people in other provinces and get-money supplied almost entirely by the people of this country generally.
My contention, Mr. Chairman, is that there should be equality of treatment under this section; that whatever money is voted and whatever measures are put into effect dealing with specific works, there should be equality of treatment as between the provinces. We need a new system along the lines of the recommendations of the Purvis commission, a national policy, so that this parliament will not have to deal with this question every year. The provinces, municipalities and local communities should help; so should these corporations referred to in this bill. We are proceeding in a haphazard manner.

This section also deals with agricultural distress. In other words this is not under section 3 a two-base or three-base vote; it is a home run for the agricultural people, who have this and five other bills under which they may receive assistance from this parliament.
As to the rules and regulations which may be made, I think he who pays the piper should call the tune, and that is the industrial provinces, which pay 82 per cent of the cash taxes. Ontario alone pays 41 per cent of the taxes, and it receives little or nothing in return. The premier of Ontario says he is not going to come to Ottawa with his hat in his hand asking for votes under this bill for a Toronto sewer, and will not contribute a cent. All kinds of federal buildings and undertakings throughout Canada are being paid for under this section, including airports, post offices and a hundred and one other things, but we do not get anything, not even pin money in Toronto and little in Ontario except votes for roads in new Ontario. I doubt if the hon. member for Parkdale would get enough to pay for a macadam road anywhere in his good roads system, and I hope he will have something to say about the matter tonight. In the light of our experience I do not believe this section ever shoidd have been passed. I venture to say that if, when this provision was first introduced, we had known how these votes would be handed out, with some places getting a great deal and others getting nothing, with some provinces paying practically nothing for relief and others paying most of the cost and getting nothing, with some provinces getting permanent works at the expense of the other provinces, we never would have adopted it.
This system should not be continued. A new system is wanted. The present system was condemned in a brief presented to the Rowell commission by the government of Ontario. That province was represented before the commission by a lawyer who presented a brief; a large sum of money was spent in preparing that brief, and it condemned the system under which a province like Ontario, which pays such a large share of the taxes, gets little or nothing in return. Under this bill Ontario is made the goat of confederation. It is not fair. The minister comes from a city in Ontario; he is rather an able young man. and I am surprised that he does not do something for his own province, or help to get Ontario to agree to the legislation. Ontario is an old province, but we do not ask for everything. I believe the principle of confederation should be what is well expressed

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
in the old Cornish battle cry, "Each for all and all for each." If something is done for the benefit of the maritimes it is for the benefit of Ontario; but when I see favouritism, with some places getting all the benefits and others getting nothing, I do not think it is fair. A person may have to pay for a roadway in front of his own property, while another municipality can have fifty per cent of the cost of a similar roadway paid under this section and part by a province. You take Fleet street and University avenue in Toronto; the city had to pay for the construction and has to maintain those roads. If we were in another province we might have fifty per cent of that cost contributed by the dominion and a further contribution by the province. The system should be changed. The minister and his officials are overworked, but I believe we should call a halt, change this system here and now, and deal directly with the larger municipalities. I think we should cease handing out money in this way at the expense of the industrial workers of Ontario and Quebec.
This is a haphazard system of handling this problem. In the prairie provinces it does not cost them anything for relief; they are getting it at the expense of the whole dominion. At the present time there are five or six other relief bills on the order paper which are intended to benefit the people of the west. I believe that during the recess of parliament the minister should carefully consider the whole system and get a new one and deal directly with the large cities. I believe that we should have a national policy to deal with unemployment and that any grants of money should be under a standard plan approved by the dominion, with whom all should meet. The late government dealt directly with Vancouver and other large cities in this country and got results. Where does the revenue come from? It comes from the industrial cities such as Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, London, Windsor, Vancouver, Winnipeg and so on, yet one of the industrial provinces, Ontario, can get none or little of this money. Under this section the minister, through the governor in council, can choose the provinces, the works and the measures. That is unfair; it is discrimination; it is not for the general advantage of Canada. We are overtaxed and over-governed in this country, yet we are continuing under this principle which was condemned in five or six briefs before the Rowell commission.

Mr. Chairman, may I add a few words in connection with relief works and the bill under discussion. I would not like to enter into an acrimonious controversy with provincial governments, but I think the government of the province of Quebec to-day raises the gratuitous accusation that the dominion government refuses its cooperation in the matter of relief works. I feel bound to take part in the discussion in order to give some facts for the information of my province so that its people may judge on their merits the opposing factions and give each one its share of responsibility.
A few years ago, after the coming into power of the conservative government in Quebec, Mr. Duplessis and some of his colleagues came to Ottawa to seek the assistance of the dominion government. If I am not mistaken, they received a grant of approximately $2,000,000 for different works. I will not attempt to mention all the projects undertaken jointly by the provincial and the federal authorities in the province of Quebec. I will refer only to project No. 17, in connection with the highway from Mont Laurier to Senneterre, which has been carried out with funds provided partly by the province and partly by the dominion. We have contributed to that project from $70,000 to $75,000, I think. An agreejnent was concluded between the two governments under which political considerations were to be excluded, and the construction of the highway would be entirely under the direction of the provincial authorities.
We succeeded, thanks to the intervention of the federal Minister of Labour, in having inspectors appointed, whose sole duty was to check the payrolls. It is unnecessary to add, Mr. Chairman, that these inspectors had no jurisdiction to point out any irregularities which might occur in the execution of the work. In the course of an interview which I had at the time with the Minister of Labour at Ottawa I expressed strong doubts regarding the sincerity of the Quebec government. As it was just after the National Union government's victories of August, 1936, we had to be very careful, the verdict of Quebec having been conclusive to a degree. However, I opposed then as I do now the Dominion government's contributing to unemployment relief works in Quebec province without having the opportunity and privilege of controlling the expenditures.
My apprehensions were justified, Mr. Chairman. I have in my hand a detailed report made by two detectives who visited the spot and found extraordinary anomalies in the

administration of the work on the highway between Mont Laurier and Senneterre on the section conducted by a man named Moore, of Maniwaki. I shall not read the report in full, but simply point out certain facts which will enlighten the people of my province as well as this government. These facts will also serve to indicate the procedure which should be followed in future. As I say, Mr. Chairman, no control was exercised over these relief works. For instance, the detectives say:
In groups of 25 to 30, the men were brought to their working place in trucks, with their belongings. As it was a long trip and the weather was bad, the trucks offered no protection against wind and cold, and the men suffered very much from the cold during that trip.
On their arrival, the men were taken to the clerk's office and, after registering, were told to report to one or several foremen under whom they were to work.

speechtext:
In the fall, I think.
The men received three pairs of woollen blankets each and slept 24 in a canvas tent measuring 16 by 24.' In some tents, the ground was covered with branches; in others, with a wood floor, on which the men had to make their bed. For a mattress, the men had to carry hay from bales piled in the yard. They did not mind breaking open several bales to get clean and dry hay.
As there was no warehouse for storing supplies, everything was lying about in the yard. There were barrels of gasoline, oil and grease, food, hay and so on. As these supplies, hay, for instance, were left without protection, the men had to carry a large quantity of wet, damp, heated or mouldy hay to find some which they could use.
Through a lack of organization, men were forced to sleep and eat in groups as best they could, with consequent indescribable disorder. One man in each tent was detailed to look after the fire during the day and another during the night. Even red hot stoves failed to keep the men warm and dry, and they often had to sleep in their wet clothes.
Sanitary conditions were non-existent. No one in authority would concern himself about them; filth was everywhere around the tents and about the camps and the air was foul with it all. Some tents were old and torn, affording no protection against the rain and cold. Poor sleeping quarters, lack of even the most elementary sanitary regulations, scarcity of balanced rations, all tended to create much discontent. Representations were made to the foremen requesting improved conditions, but without avail.
Failing any organization and with everyone having ready access to supplies, pilfering on a high scale was an easy matter. Men would go and take woollen blankets, obtaining more than they were entitled to. Wagon and truck drivers also helped themselves. They would often take new ones on each succeeding trip and they would not be seen bringing back the old ones.

The report goes on to state that a foreman by the name of Jos. Poirier said that about 1,100 woollen blankets had vanished and that he had been unable to trace them.
