speechtext: Eleven hundred pairs of blankets?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yes, 1,100 pair, 2,200 blankets. And that is not all:
There was too much of certain foodstuffs and not enough of others, so that, at first, meals were not properly balanced. The rate of 90 cents per day for board and lodging was deemed prohibitive with the result that strikes and disturbances were impending. After some representations had been made to the foremen rates were reduced to 50 cents per day.
And further, Mr. Chairman:
Camp No. 1, that is, the main division which was the centre of the works and equipment consisted in 22 frame buildings.
Those buildings had been built with funds provided by both governments. I continue:
A portable saw-mill was brought and used in connection with the logs cut down in the nearby forest. Huge quantities of boards were used in building some of the shacks. As they were available in such large quantities, the waste was considerable. It is impossible to give figures which might afford even an approximate estimate of the money spent on wasted lumber. Organization and coordination were lacking altogether. Whenever a piece of board was needed, it was cut from a full length board and the remainder thrown away. No control was exercised on the job by the foremen, which explains much of the waste. Buildings were erected in other camps under the same wasteful conditions.
In camp No. 1, the first buildings that were erected were for the use of Superintendent Atkinson and the clerk, after which stables, stores and warehouses were built. The buildings in which the men were to be housed were the last to be erected. This was a cause of dissatisfaction among the men who claimed that animals had precedence over them. However, the teamsters stated that the men already had tents at their disposal, that their horses had no shelter and could not be left out of doors after a hard day's work, that the canvas shelters set up for the horses were too damp and that it was preferable to leave the latter in the open lest they should become sick.
In camps No. 2 and No. 3, decayed lumber was used for the erection of buildings. Too large quantities of that material had been taken there and left unsheltered in the open. The carpenters had to use it for building the shacks. In that camp, as well as in the others, materials and provisions were left in the open, with the result that a large quantity of them was spoilt and later had to be thrown away. Kegs of nails which were still nearly full had been left uncovered and the contents had rusted in the rain. Being useless, the nails were left there. Kegs were opened indiscriminately, and the contents of many of them were spilt over the ground. Such facts were reported to the foremen, but the waste continued unchecked.
That camp was in a state of utter confusion. No one invested with authority took the trouble of doing anything to prevent such abuses.
Mr. Chairman, I could quote the whole report, but I do not want to take up more time. What I. wish to show is that there was no semblance of organization in those relief works and that the federal government was justified in refusing to make any furthei contribution towards works of that character. I even claim, Mr. Chairman, that if the federal authorities had continued to follow that course, they would, in my opinion, have been party to robbery and graft. Some 50 men from the constituency of Labelle were given work on project No. 17.
Other men remain on the job with the intention of doing as little as possible and avoiding work whenever they could.
The group from Three Rivers-
Incidentally, I may say that a number of unemployed from Three Rivers were sent to this district, thus displacing the unemployed of Labelle and Gatineau counties.

conducted to the office of assistant superintendent J. Poirier informed the latter and anyone else who would listen that they had been sent by Maurice and that they had not come there to work. If that does not suit you, they said, let us know and we will see about it. Faced with that ultimatum J. Poirier is reported to have told them not to get excited and that he would look after them. They were assigned to foreman J. Turpin. Not one of them was ever seen to do a stroke of work and one of them was heard to say on several occasions: "I broke an axehandle and the whole bunch of us have not done enough work to pay for it." They had been placed in a camp by themselves and were well fed. Finally, tiring of their idle life and wishing to visit some of the other camps, they asked to be sent elsewhere, which was done. Before leaving they said one of them would remain behind in order to bring them their mail and run errands between this camp and the other places to which they might go. This was granted to them and some time after their return one of them said that he was disgusted with the way things were managed.
There is more, Mr. Chairman, and this is an example of the scandal which I feel I should bring to the attention of the government.
Shortly after the holidays the assistant superintendent's son, L. Poirier, arrived at the camp. He was not given any work nor was he assigned to any foreman. He received the wages of a carpenter working eight hours a day. He spent all his time making wooden tool chests which he sold for $3 each. These tool boxes, made of one-inch red pine, were 3 feet long, 16 inches wide and 15 inches deep. They were made on government time and with government material. The metal fittings for the said chests were likewise made, on government time and with government material, by blacksmith Rondeau who worked in camps No. 1, 2 and 3. Some 200 tool chests were made and sold to the workmen. They were made not secretly but openly, although Poirier claimed that he made them during his spare time

Nobody protested, it being desirable to remain friendly with the assistant superintendent's son.

Our inspectors, who prepared the report, found that bags of potatoes were discarded after having been carried in the cold weather in open vehicles so that they might freeze. About ten carcasses of pork and ten of beef were retrieved, as well as some bacon and boxes of sausages. You realize, Mr. Chairman, the appalling waste that was going on. I must apologize for using such picturesque language, but those are facts we must know and which caused the Minister of Labour to abandon relief works of that kind. I objected to them at the time and I am still opposed to them. I would even go as far as to say that I am expressing the opinion of my fellow-members from the province of Quebec. We are in favour of relief works for alleviating unemployment, but I think it is only fair that their whole administration should be left to the dominion government.
Mr. Chairman, I shall not proceed any further with the recital of such abuses, but if

honourable members who are interested in these facts care for further details, I shall undertake to furnish them with more particulars that are not to the credit of those who are responsible for these relief works. Besides, we are in a position to prove that a certain political organization compelled truck owners to buy "Diamond T" trucks; otherwise, they could not obtain work on the Mont-Laurier43enneterre highway. The party selling those trucks was a strong supporter of the Union Nationale party in Papineau county. We find the same conditions in the county of Labelle, where an official of the department of colonization of the province of Quebec, at Mont Laurier, is the agent for those trucks. He tells people: "If you buy your trucks from me, you will get work on the Mont Laurier and Senneterre highway." Do you think, Mr. Chairman, that, in such circumstances, the federal government can, decently, offer its cooperation to the Quebec government? We have a hundred reasons, not to refuse our cooperation, but to insist on a different system for the distribution of public funds appropriated for unemployment relief works.
I now wish to discuss another matter. Parliament passed an act authorizing the government to lend money to municipalities, up to a total of 830,000,000, at an interest rate of 2 per cent. Had the province of Quebec accepted that plan, as most of the other provinces did, we would have obtained money at a low rate for local improvements. The parish of Ferme-Neuve in my county had to borrow money for the building of sewers at 5 per cent instead of 2 per cent because the provincial government, for no reason at all, would not cooperate with the federal government. Their objection was that guarantees were required. I say that such guarantees were essential to make those loans regular under our constitution, and the Quebec government could have given them without any risk, because the decision as to the amount in each case rested with the provincial authorities alone.
I now come to the loans under the home improvement plan. There were 44,941 such loans amounting to $18,695,511.99 for cities with a population of 5.000 or over. The total number of loans under the home improvement plan was 63,516 amounting to $25,340,305.63. In that field, the federal government helped in relieving unemployment.
I Shall next bring another matter to the attention of the government. Last year, thanks to the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) and to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), my constituency had the

In conclusion, I trust that there will soon be an end to the practice of making political capital out of the sufferings of the people and that all governments will take the necessary steps to prevent speculation at the expense of those who are starving.
I thank the Minister of Labour for the consideration he has given to my constituency in the matter of relief works. maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with the greatest attention to the speech just delivered by my distinguished colleague from Labelle (Mr. Lalonde). This afternoon, I had listened to the constitutional theories presented by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. It is evident that the constitution must be flexible. Ocean liners very often change their course to rush to the rescue of a floundering ship.
Such may be the case of the dominion government in the trying conditions we are experiencing.
There have always been two schools of jurists. Rome had its Proculians and Sabinians, even as we have to-day. Some of our colleagues belonging' to the legal profession favour a very strict interpretation of the law, while others wish for greater liberality. In certain respects the constitution should foe amended so as to allow freer action on the part of the dominion government, provided it be proven necessary. At present, however,
I observe that federal and provincial governments alike are acting with regard to unemployment as if there were no constitution, and it is only when a government wants to refuse some request that the British North America Act is invoked.
Should we wish to keep to a strict interpretation of the British North America Act, the dominion government must perforce maintain peaceful relations with the provincial governments, if both intend to cooperate. That is elementary. And in that event it is absolutely necessary to open negotiations not through the League of Nations, but through voluntary intermediaries, to the end that all differences between the federal and provincial governments may be ironed out. If that is done, the greatly desired harmony referred to this afternoon by an hon. member from the Social Credit group will be achieved. It is not a difficult matter. It is a question, first of all, of ascertaining the wishes of everyone, instead of avoiding one another and acting like enemies. The Prime Minister may have to throw out ballast. That is commonly done; when we want to rise, we have to throw out a little ballast. It might not be such a bad thing to throw out some ballast also, for the sake of peace.
But should peace be impossible, there is another way. If the dominion and provincial governments cannot agree upon joint works, let them each undertake their share in connection with certain projects. In the matter of the trans-Canada highway, for instance, if the dominion and provincial governments cannot agree upon the joint construction of a certain section of the highway, why not divide it into sections and let the dominion and provincial governments build each a section alternately? The parishes could be divided in two. Half the work in a parish could be performed by the federal government and the other half by the provincial government. This suggestion is made in case the dominion and provincial governments should find it impossible to reach an agreement. That is a suggestion. Even though mountains cannot meet, it should foe
Un

employment and Agricultural Distress
quite easy for two men to come together for a friendly discussion of matters in which they are mutually interested.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: There are not two mountains, but a mountain and a precipice.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I do not quite agree with my honourable friend. There is such a thing as freedom of opinion. He has a perfect right to hold his own views.
We will have either to reach an agreement or hit upon some accurate definition of what we are to do. I regret greatly that no agreement could be reached in connection with the settlers in spite of the good will shown by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and even the willingness displayed by Mr. Hereford, who must not be mistaken for Mr. Dickson, to whom I was referring this afternoon. The minister and Mr. Hereford will remember the exhaustive inquiry which was held in the county of Temiscouata. Investigators from the federal Department of Labour interviewed from 1,200 to 1,400 families of settlers in this county in order to ascertain the conditions. It was at my request that the inquiry was held. They witnessed the distress of those settlers. I afterwards took the trouble to conduct an inquiry of my own in order to find out how many animals those people had on their farms. Some of them had six animals-six hens. Others had but one animal-a dog. A great many settlers had no oxen, horses, sheep or hens. How could they farm under such conditions? Their predicament is appalling. These settlers were placed there quite a long time ago, not under the present administration, but before, following the division of colonization lots from maps which did not show the altitude of the land. These maps, which were as level as the floor, gave no indication of the land elevation. Thus it is that there are settlers on mountain slopes and others on mountain tops. In the parish of St. Jean de la Lande, in the southern part of my county, there are seven mountains on each one of which are to be found two or three small houses. To visit their neighbours, the settlers have to descend an enormous hill and ascend another one. Then there is the precipice to which my hon. friend referred a moment ago. Because of its seven hills I call St. Jean de la Lande the eternal city.
These settlers are leading very precarious lives and I have called the attention of the country to their plight. I am grateful to the newspapers which published my representations on their behalf. I have also brought their case to the attention of all the governments of the province of Quebec, and 
I am sorry to see, Mr. Chairman, that a man who is responsible for the distress of these settlers in my county still occupies a very important position in the provincial colonization service. He is a dangerous man. I have denounced him on several occasions but neither the former nor the present government have given me the amounts paid to him by the Canadian National Railways while he was in their employ.
But these settlers are suffering, they are poverty-stricken, and we must help them. Cannot the dominion government give a special grant to the provincial government so as to help these worthy people? The situation is known to the minister, he has the report. Mr. Hereford has read it. It was very well prepared by officials of the Department of Labour, who are not numerous, but quite competent. I am deeply indebted to Mr. Hereford, as well as to Messrs. Carter, Lafortune-a former controller of the city of Ottawa-and Pigeon. This report I had asked for and those gentlemen found that these settlers needed help; I hope they get it.
Mr. Chairman, if we are to obtain appropriations for relief works, I hope that peace may reign anew so that our friends who may not be supporters of the provincial government may also have their share of work. Personally, I have no reason to complain of the provincial government which has shown itself very generous when time came to help the unemployed in my constituency by having repairs made to the lock at Morin lake. I trust the dominion government will also contribute to the rebuilding of these locks which are exceedingly important from the point of view of flood control. The matter is extremely important. The minister is well aware of that, he knows the situation and I hope he is now listening attentively to this wholly legitimate request.
Something should be done for our young people, not only to enable them to take up courses, but also to afford them transportation for that purpose, and we should see to it that at the end of their period of training they may benefit from the knowledge so acquired.
Many young people have read in the papers that the government was planning to spend one million dollars for the technical training of youth. The minister will remember that when the matter was first brought up in 1936, the hon. member for Temiscouata pointed out how important it was to bring home to the young people the necessity of respecting craftsmen. Nowadays, no consideration is shown to craftsmen. Our educational system is, to a great extent, responsible for that.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
The training which our young people receive only qualifies them for clerical work. We have clerks in untold numbers; they are as numerous as grasshoppers. Our young people will not take up trades which are quite respectable and useful to society. Machines are displacing manual labour, and with their commercial training, our youths refuse to take up honest trades. We will, have to go back to the old times; we will have to respect, as we formerly did, those who produce our wearing apparel: the tailors, the shoemakers, the haberdashers, in short, all those who are plying some honest trade of any description. Our educational institutions should also teach our children from their earliest years to respect craftsmen, because they are absolutely necessary to our economic life.
Two years ago, in England, I had the privilege of visiting stately buildings admission to which is usually denied to tourists and more particularly to American tourists. I refer to the Guild buildings, which are remnants of the guilds of the Middle Ages. One can see there the great part played by corporations in England. They are immensely wealthy institutions which have contributed in a remarkable way to the teaching of crafts. For instance, the former prime minister Ramsay MacDonald himself attended a school founded and maintained by the guilds. In England, trades are held in high regard, and the strength of that country is based on the middle classes which are the backbone of the nation.
Conditions will not be improved in Canada by the teaching of learned theories, but by a return to the three R's. It is useless to think that unemployment will disappear overnight. The Canadian people will have, in the first place, to re-educate themselves, to return to the principles of former times when people respected that which was worthy of respect. We should not start a book by the end, as they do in China-but by the beginning, by the rudiments.
One of the first things to do in order to put our country on the right path is to teach our youth to respect the crafts and encourage them to practise them.
Then, Mr. Chairman, we must not allow our fellow-citizens to starve. Although some have painted too dark a picture of the situation, it must be admitted that there are some very sad cases. A brilliant Montreal journalist, Mr. Richer, recently mentioned things that are occurring daily in Ottawa, a city which should be less affected than others by unemployment, owing to the millions of dollars paid in salaries to the civil servants. Only yesterday, a young man came to my door and told me that he had a family to
support and that his little daughter and himself had not had anything to eat all day. That is happening in the city of Ottawa. The Ottawa people are very well disposed, they are charitable, but there is something lacking. Members of the clergy have united to establish an association for the purpose of feeding under-nourished school children. That is very fine, that is admirable, but there again such marks of devotion should not be necessary.
I mean, Mr. Chairman, that in a city like this one, such cases of distress should not exist. The federal government should get into touch with the provincial government and the Ottawa municipal authorities with a view to improving the situation. It seems quite feasible to me, but how can it be done if, as I stated this afternoon, we only care for those who are classed as unemployed? Inadequate care is taken of the white collared, educated needy. Up to the present time, only those appearing on the direct relief lists or those who are on relief works have been considered as unemployed. Young men who are 16, 17, 20 or 25 years of age, with some schooling, but who have never been employed, are not classed among unemployed. They are not unemployed the minute their father holds a temporary job or if he earns regularly a few dollars a week. That is an injustice, Mr. Chairman, I take it. I believe that we should class among the unemployed not only those receiving relief allowances or employed on relief works, but also those who at times earn a little, but who cannot make a decent living. They are the ones who are unfortunate and who nurse the greatest worries, for their children being unable to find work, they cannot see any future for them.
I realize that the government is faced with a very difficult task; I admit that the government cannot be compared to "Santa Claus" and find work for all the unemployed, whether they are on relief or not, but, on the other hand, before the government is in a position to give further help, it is absolutely necessary that the chief officials of the Department of Labour give leadership to the nation, and ' that we teach in the schools that a trade is an honourable occupation and also that paternalism, far from contributing to the welfare of the people, is dangerous, and can operate only for the benefit of the few. I trust, therefore, that in dealing with unemployment we shall do so as objectively as possible, not for the purpose of justifying or condemning the policy of one party as against that of another, but in the interest of those who suffer, so as to improve their lot and rid every home of that feeling of anxiety which is a constant threat to peace in this country.

speechtext:
This section reads:
The governor in council may enter into agreements :
(a)	with any of the provinces respecting the alleviation of unemployment conditions and of agricultural distress therein and to assist those in need;
(b)	with corporations or partnerships or individuals engaged in industry respecting the expansion of industrial employment.
I think these two parts should go together. The word "expansion" might act as a deterrent to the minister in granting any increase or help which he may be disposed to give. I suggest that this phraseology be changed to read in one clause something like this: "With any of the provinces respecting alleviation of unemployment conditions and with corporations or partnerships or with individuals engaged in industry respecting industrial employment and agricultural distress." That would cover the situation in a proper manner. I cannot see why the industrial sections of the country should not be considered as on a parity with the agricultural sections in the matter of distress. We have more distress in our manufacturing centres in the cities than we have in the country. It seems to me that every endeavour is being made to assist agricultural distress, and I maintain that industrial distress in the cities should be properly looked after and eliminated. I believe this could be done if the minister would assist the industrialists to provide employment. I should like the minister to take into consideration this matter of giving greater attention to the cities.

This same clause was in the bill which was before the house last year. Actually it

has not been invoked except on one rather recent occasion, when agreements were entered into with the railway companies at the time the relief camps were closed.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I had reference to the part having to do with expansion. I do not think it is necessary to say for expansion or for any other particular purpose; I believe the purpose should be to give assistance to corporations, partnerships or individuals engaged in industry, with respect to industrial employment. I believe the words "the expansion" should be deleted. That is the point I was trying to make.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I want to endorse paragraph (b) of this section. In bringing forward this measure, the minister is only doing what is being done in other countries. I would not ask for assistance to industry if the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) were correct. He apparently embraced all industry, but I do not think he meant that; I assume he meant that there was an occasional industrialist who did not play the game. That may be quite true, but I certainly do not endorse his all-embracing statement that industry is the soulless outfit that I understood the hon. member to class it. I was associated with industry for a long time, and I know that by far the majority of the managers and executives of industry came from the ranks of industry itself. These men had the very same souls when they were working in industry that they had when they became managers or executives. My experience on the whole has been that the industrialists of Canada as a class are as Godfearing and sincefe as any men to be found in any walk of life, I care not what it is.
Believing that, I want to support whatever can be done under paragraph (b), because the Canadian manufacturer who exports his products is up against certain conditions that may be alleviated under this section. For example, in Great Britain to-day a company exporting goods to the continent-and I will take electrical companies, or companies manufacturing lines of equipment that require electrical parts, because I am familiar with such companies, although this would apply to all other industries as well-must assure importers on the continent that at least fifty per cent of the material entering into the article exported has its origin in the old country. This has resulted in quite a number of Canadian companies being compelled to establish branch plants in the old country. I visited a number of these branches of Canadian companies which formerly enjoyed a
considerable export business to European countries. This, of course, has meant a loss of employment in Canada. I have in mind one company that now has in London a larger plant than the parent concern in Toronto. Formerly the Toronto plant shipped all the goods exported to European countries; to-day those exports are sent from the English plant, because of the regulations pertaining to manufacture in the old country. So, if any assistance can be given under this section, to the remaining plants in Canada, they certainly need it in these times, and it would mean a good deal of employment.
To continue with the plant I have in mind, it costs a great deal less to manufacture in London than in Toronto. The London plant has a floor space of approximately 12,000 square feet, most of which is on the one floor. It costs only $175 a year to heat that plant. The parent plant in Toronto is perhaps a little smaller, but on account of our climatic conditions it costs far more to heat the Toronto plant; I believe the figure is approximately $800 a year. That is one item. Another item is the wage bill. In Great Britain, as the minister knows, under the youth unemployment relief regulations young folk working in industry are partly paid by contributions from whatever government department it is that encourages the employment of youth in the old country. I visited one factory which employed several thousand youths from fourteen to sixteen years of age, who received on an average a pound a week. I knew they could not live on a pound a week, and I inquired from one of the managers how the difference was made up. He told me the youths received, in addition to the pound a week earned, a contribution from some government department or fund the name of which I have forgotten, sufficient to make up the difference between what they required and what they were paid in that industry.
I do not know whether we have anything like that in Canada. I do know that a boy fourteen years of age in this country is not allowed to work at all; as I understand it, he must be sixteen years old before he can go to work. That is not the ease in the old country, however, and there the cost of production is lower than it is here. Perhaps under this section the department could figure out some way to assist industry in Canada to cut down production costs.
I found out that one of the labour offices, I believe it was the King's Cross labour office, had applications for over 12,000 between the ages of fourteen and sixteen. Evidently the manufacturers of the old country are taking

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
advantage of the assistance from the government to enable them to employ youths for the purpose of manufacturing operations. The machines operated are so perfectly constructed that to-day a fourteen year old boy can operate a machine to make 6-inch shells, and turn them out as rapidly and as efficiently as a man could do. The machines are perfected to such a point that they do practically all the work. I saw youths operating large shell machines.
We cannot do that in Canada. Therefore there is an avenue where something could be done. I do not know just how far the department can go, but it is evident that the employment of youth in the old country must be detrimental to the operations of exporters in this country. Perhaps the department has ' something of the kind in mind.
Probably the minister is aware that in Germany there is a two i ter cent tax on all manufactured goods. That tax goes into a common pool, and in every instance where a German manufacturer has to export at a price lower than he otherwise should, he withdraws compensation from the pool. I do not think we would want that system here; possibly this could not be done in Canada. However, I point it out as one condition which reduces exports from Canada, and consequently reduces opportunities for labour.
The minister also will be aware that recently the government of the United States voted many millions of dollars to assist in the exportation of manufactured products. I have been told, further, that Swedish manufacturers can obtain any order they want. Of course they do not get them all, but they obtained one recently in Canada. I am told by a manufacturer that a Swedish company obtained an order for $50,000 worth of electrical goods. That may not be considered a large order, but it is a substantial one. He informed me that the Swedish manufacturers are in a position to obtain any order they wish to go after.
Therefore I am in accord with what I believe to be the import of paragraph (b). I would agree with the paragraph if the import of it is to assist i dustry, under certain conditions which the department of Labour and the Department of Trade and Commerce would approve. As I say, if the import of paragraph (b) is to enable industry in Canada to keep its men employed as much as possible and, where necessary, to increase its personnel, then to my way of thinking it is a very good provision.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
May I take the opposite point of view from that taken by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Clarke):	I
think there may be some justification for doing what is suggested in the paragraph, alI Mr. MacNicol.]
though I am not sure about it. I refer to the provision to assist private corporations in the expansion of their industry. But I cannot see any reason why we should place-

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It says, "expansion of
industrial employment."

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Yes, but the interpretation placed upon those words was somewhat different.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
The hon. member surely
is not opposed to increasing employment.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I always listen to the
hon. member for Davenport with a good deal of interest and respect, because he makes a practice of conducting personal investigations with respect to various matters, and then brings to the house information based upon those investigations. That is a procedure which, I think, is worth while. However, I should like to say this, in the absence of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis), that perhaps the interpretation placed upon the words he used this afternoon was not the correct one. If my recollection serves me correctly, the words of the hon. member were to the effect that there were some good employers who had never worked in industry for hire themselves. I do not think the statement was as sweeping as would appear from the interpretation placed upon it by the hon. member for Davenport.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I am glad somebody
else got a different impression.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
On the other hand
there was some justification for what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver East. It so happened that while hon. members were speaking in the French language this evening, and as unfortunately I do not understand it very well especially when it is spoken rapidly, I took occasion to examine a copy of a magazine published in Toronto by the youth movement of Canada. While the hon. members were speaking, I was reading an article entitled Textiles, and from it I shall quote one or two extracts. It is written by a textile worker, and this statement is made:
The average age of men in this industry is 25-26 years, and that of women 24 years, which, even if they look old, does not take them out of the "youth" class.
Then this statement is made to which I draw particular attention:
The international labour office at Geneva says that in 1931 twelve of every hundred Canadian textile workers were 10-17 years of age. A study of the cotton and woollen industries of Ontario conducted by the Toronto office of our union (United Textile Workers) at the beginning of 1938, shows no change in this figure.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
Then it goes on to say that there are some 65,000 persons employed in these mills, and some of the conditions are given. I shall quote again:
It would take more than a mere genius to become inspired or enthused when after 54J hours of work in one week the pay envelope contains $7.26.
Then an instance is given of working seventy-eight hours in one week, and it is stated that girls are paid 11J cents an hour. After a 52-hour week they find that they have less than S6 to pay their weekly board bill. Conditions like that justify what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver East.
I am not going to quote more from the article, although I could do so. Of course the comment made is that the textile industry was investigated by the Turgeon commission. The industry itself is protected and to that degree of course is subsidized, and has created fortunes for some of the owners.
When we have industries of that description, it seems to me the criticisms that are sometimes levelled against industries-perhaps in too general a form-are justified at least to some extent. I think the minister in endeavouring to expand employment is to be congratulated, provided that in the expansion the interests of the countiy are properly safeguarded. I know that the railways were, shall I say bonused, by having work done several years ago by people on relief. I was thoroughly in accord with that being done for our national railway, but I am not so sure that we are justified in doing it for private corporations to the extent that some advocate. I would rather see a program confined to public works of various descriptions. I would point out that in the United States WPA works and other forms of public works have absorbed many thousands of the unemployed and have given to the people not only the necessities but many of the amenities of community life. I should like to see more of that sort of thing done in the dominion.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I do not rise to make any complaint with reference to clause 4 of this bill, although it seems to me it is hardly broad enough to cover all sections of this country. Clause 4 reads:
The governor in council may enter into agreements:
(a) with any of the provinces respecting the alleviation of unemployment conditions and of agricultural distress therein.
I assume that means distress in the drought areas of the west. We have no objection to the large sums of money that have been spent in the west; but there has been great distress
among the fishermen of the maritime provinces, and it occurs to me that this clause should be broad enough to cover the fishing as well as the agricultural industry. Would it not be possible to enlarge this clause to take in the fishing industry? We know there has been some difference of opinion as between the federal government and some of the local governments in connection with the alleviation of distress conditions in this industry, and I thought possibly it could be included under this clause.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: There is no question that under this clause agreements could be entered into by which assistance could be given to those in need in the fishing industry. The hon. member should note the last words in the clause, "and to assist those in need." While those words refer with greater particularity to unemployment and agricultural distress, they do not preclude us from giving assistance to the fishermen. I would say also that the provision for agricultural distress has not been confined to the western provinces. I refer to one particular agreement, which for two years was under the Department of Labour but which has been transferred to the Department of Agriculture, under which assistance is given in New Brunswick for the reestablishment of settlers. I mention this simply to show that agreements with respect to agricultural distress are not confined to the western provinces.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Apparently, under this clause, agreements are made with the provinces?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Correct.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Would it not be possible to have in the agreements a standard provision with reference to residence, setting out just how long a person must reside in a province in order to establish residence? As I understand it, there are different conditions prevailing in the different provinces and the need for some uniformity is extremely great. I would refer the hon. minister to a publication of the Canadian welfare council entitled "Wayfarers Perforce," which was issued in February, 1939. On page 13 I find these words:
. . . the conclusion is inevitable, time and time again, that, in order to provide for the orderly administration of our social services, some attempt must be made to clarify the question of what constitutes residence, either municipally or provincially, and to bring about the acceptance of something like uniformity in the definition of residence in this dominion.
The minister has apparently had inserted in the agreements a paragraph dealing with municipal residence within the province. For
3038	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
instance, in section 5 of the agreement with British Columbia dated July 19, 1938, there is this provision:
The province agrees to maintain such residence regulations that no person shall become ineligible to receive material aid by reason of having lost residence in one municipality or jurisdiction within the province before having established residence in another.
Would it not be possible to make it a condition of these grants in aid that each province should adopt standard residence rules to be set by the dominion?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: That particular suggestion of my hon. friend is now under discussion with the provincial governments. The agreements with the various provinces with respect to the grants in aid can become operative only after this legislation has received royal assent. The agreements are made operative under this legislation. I may say that a similar discussion took place yesterday when the point was raised by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) and his colleague the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I gave those hon. gentlemen the same answer I am giving now, namely that this question of domicile and transiency is being canvassed very carefully.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: In view of the fact the money comes from the dominion, is this government not in a position to insist that such a standard provision be adopted by each province? Must it necessarily be a matter of agreement?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: It is always possible for us to attach conditions to our grants in aid, but in administrative practice it is not always possible to make such conditions entirely effective. I can assure my hon. friend that we are going as far as we can in bringing about uniformity, but he will recognize that the question of domicile is under provincial jurisdiction. It is questionable just how far the provinces would be willing to abandon the position they have taken with respect to domicile unless they could be persuaded that it was in their interest and in the interest of the country as a whole to do so.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: If they could not get the money otherwise, they could easily be persuaded.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Is it compulsory for the province to put in an amount equal to that contributed by the dominion government in connection with any work to alleviate distress?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is not compulsory that the amount contributed by the province to a

work program shall be equal to the contribution of the dominion government. Normally that is the case, but sometimes the provinces have preferred that the dominion contribution should be spread over a larger program; at times it has been applied to the direct labour costs of projects. There has not been an entirely uniform practice in that respect.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
What I had in mind was the application of the city of Toronto for aid in connection with the construction of a sewage disposal plant which is very necessary at the present time. It seems to me that when one looks over the brief-the minister probably has a copy-he must see that this project is more in the nature of that referred to in section 3 as being in the general interest of Canada. Toronto, having expended so much for relief in the past few years, has come to the point where its borrowing power has been reduced to some $7,000,000.	In the
United States, cities near the border that were forced to put in seiwage disposal plants received aid from the federal government, and I think it would come well from the federal government here to advance some money towards this project in Toronto in spite of the fact that the province has, I understand, refused to advance any money in equal proportions with the dominion government.
I would point out that Toronto has contributed to the federal treasury in the past six years $296,277,576 in customs revenue, $42,662,830 in postal revenue, and $154,848,143 in income tax, or a total of $493,788,550, although it cannot be segregated for that city alone. Certainly something will have to be done in connection with this sewage disposal plant, because it is very much overloaded at the present time and the waters of the lake are being polluted; and as I said in the house last year, this is having a bad effect on the fish. It is more of a dominion than a provincial matter. It is probably more between a federal and a municipal project than it is a provincial project. Cannot some aid from the federal government be given at least to get this project started? It is a necessary work and would contribute greatly to relieving the terrible unemployment condition in Toronto to-day.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Would it not be possible for the department to work out a scheme to take care of border-line cases of people who cannot qualify by reason of residence? The provinces do not agree on residence; and, until they do, could not these border-line cases become temporarily the sole responsibility of the dominion in much the same way as transients are so regarded? It

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
causes me a great deal of unhappiness to think that such cases as I referred to this afternoon should exist. The woman is in the greatest danger of 'being cut right off from all sources of relief, which is distressing to the widowed mother of a family of children, where she usually has anxiety enough without being faced with a situation of that sort. I feel that some regulation should be made to cover such cases, and perhaps the minister would tell us what is being done in that respect.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I shall certainly take note
of the case which my hon. friend brought to the attention of the house this afternoon and see whether the responsibility of the government can be determined with respect to that particular woman and her family. If all the provinces would enter into an arrangement with the dominion government for an equal division of the cost of relief of transients there would be no residual transients, as my hon. friend will understand, and we hope we can bring the provinces to that point of view. Personally I have always preferred to seek that kind of cooperative measure rather than to . adopt a policy which might create a group of what might be termed dominion transients. Domicile, after all, is essentially a provincial matter, and there is no territory in this country short of the Northwest Territories which is not also provincial.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
To follow up my
question of a few moments ago, would it not be possible under this bill for the federal government to make some arrangement with the city of Toronto that would enable this work to be started even though the province has refused to cooperate?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It has never been customary to deal with particular projects in committee because, as I think my hon. friend will realize, that would produce an impossible situation. There have been some general references from my own side of the house to special projects, and I have dealt with them all in precisely the same manner. The project to which my hon. friend refers is one which would normally be referred to the dominion government through the provincial government. It has been so referred, but without any indication of the attitude of the provincial government towards the project itself. I would be quite wrong in encouraging my hon. friend to believe that there can be an acceptance by the dominion government of financial responsibility in any large
[Mr. Blackmore.)
degree for a project of the dimensions that he has indicated. As I recall it, the expenditure contemplated is in the vicinity of $16,000,000.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
The point I
wished to make was:	If Ontario does not
make application and Toronto does, then in view of the fact that this project is, to my mind, more in the nature of a harbour project, certainly not a direct municipal project, but something that is'forced on Toronto by treaty, would it. not be possible for the dominion government, under the circumstances prevailing to-day, to enter into an arrangement with Toronto so that a portion of this work might be gone on with without the matter having to go through the province?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
In any apportionment of
funds made available under this measure for civic improvements in Ontario, we shall have to consider the situation in the province as a whole in order that there may be as fair as possible an allocation of the funds among the various centres of population where unemployment exists in an acute degree. I am sorry that I cannot go beyond what I have already said with respect to the possibility of a dominion contribution towards a section of this sewage project in Toronto.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: As I understood him, the minister said that in some instances there was an equal contribution by the provinces, and that in other instances there was no contribution by the provinces. Why, in this instance, make an exception of the city of Toronto? Am I right when I say that there is no contribution by some of the provinces?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not understood me correctly when he states that I said in some instances there was no contribu-
3040	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
tion by the provinces. I said that different methods of contribution had been adopted under the various agreements with the provinces and that no compulsion in the matter has been exercised by the dominion government. We have applied our own appropriations for relief works to programs of such works submitted to us by the provincial governments. Sometimes those works were provincial; sometimes they were municipal. But there has been, I think, invariably a contribution from the provincial government. I can recall one exception to that, where certain work was done on a playground in the city of Toronto, but that was done under an agreement with the provincial government, not directly by agreement with the municipality.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Earlier this evening the minister referred to the differences in the methods of applying these grants in aid in the various provinces. For example, Ontario applied its grant in a certain way, whereas Quebec did it in another way. May I ask, in the making of these agreements with the provinces, do the provinces state the manner in which the grant in aid will be applied?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
No. Actually the clause in the agreement governs the manner in which the grant in aid is expended. In its present form that agreement was recommended by the national employment commission. The clause is as follows:
Whenever used in this agreement or any schedule thereof, the word "minister" shall mean the Minister of Labour for Canada and the term "material aid" shall mean either food, fuel, clothing and shelter (or any of them) supplied to individuals in necessitous circumstances, or, the costs of carrying on works or training projects specifically designated by the province as projects intended to provide such individuals when employed thereon (other than supervisory personnel) the equivalent of food, fuel, clothing and shelter (or any of them) which otherwise would have to be supplied to those individuals, provided in each ease that a schedule setting forth a description of the project, the estimated total cost thereof and the specific cost to which the dominion will contribute has been approved in writing by the minister.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: But there is nothing in there about rates of wages, rates of pay and so on?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Essentially we are buying a pig in a poke. It is up to the province to do anything it wishes?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No. There is another clause which provides that fair wages shall be paid.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Does that apply to a scale of wages which is not a relief scale but current rates of pay for that type of work?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Sometimes by agreement provinces have carried on what might be termed relief works. That is to say, those who work earn their relief with a certain oremium over and above what normally they would receive for relief. But one must remember tL*t the question of wages is under provincial legislation.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Quite so.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: And there has to be a certain amount of accommodation of these plans to a variety of provincial conditions.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: In regard to hostels for the transient unemployed, is the cost of hostels maintained in part under this grant as well, or is that a separate matter?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Not under the grant in aid, as a general rule, although there would be nothing to exclude it. Sometimes special arrangements are made for single unemployed men in hostels through a grant which is made available under the item in the supplementary estimates which was before the committee just before adjournment last night, that is the item for assistance to single unemployed persons.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: That is why I asked the question. I did not know whether it came from this grant or the other.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: For the most part I should say that, now we have reached the new percentage basis, those in hostels will qualify under that fifty per cent for transients.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Then it would seem to me desirable that there should be some federal supervision of these hostels if we are paying for them in part-forty per cent, or whatever it may be. At the moment is there any supervision?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No. That has not been the practice at any time in the past. The hostels are visited from time to time by officials of the Department of Labour. As a matter of fact I have visited hostels in most of our provinces, and occasionally our inspectors will bring to our attention any complaints with respect to these hostels. I am bound to say that as regards those I have visited I have formed the impression that they were being carefully administered, and certainly there was no reason to believe that those charged in the provinces with relief administration would be less careful than would similar officials responsible direct to the dominion government.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: So far as the minister recalls, have there been any complaints?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I recall no recent complaint. We do have from time to time a

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
report sent to us from the provincial governments. I speak particularly of Manitoba, where there are periodic inspections by medical boards and also by a committee of the citizens. Broadly speaking, I believe that these hostels are carried out efficiently and achieve their objectives. That does not mean that food reaches every standard of adequacy; but so far as I have seen them they have been clean and the food has been good. As a matter of fact the menus are not far different from those which were given to those who served during the great war. On the whole I would say that menus in hostels compare rather favourably with the food that was available to at least private soldiers in the late war.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What hostel in Toronto has been inspected?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I am not in a position to say that. I have not myself visited hostels in Toronto.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I wish to say one word more in connection with that sewage disposal plant. Lake Ontario, as we all know, is a boundary water, and therefore the matter is, as I said before, more a matter for the dominion. Now, on account of the treaty of 1909, Toronto is forced to take care of its sewage disposal so that the water will not be polluted, and as well as that, of course, the safety of citizens of the dominion who come there by train or air or water and so on is endangered if the water is not pure. point out again that to my mind it is more a matter for the dominion and the city of Toronto than it is to any great extent for the province of Ontario.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I was going to ask if the appropriations under this bill cover the kind of relief work which is being done in Saint John, New Brunswick and to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) referred last night. If so, it seems to me that the federal government, in making appropriations, should lay down some regulations in connection with the payments. I have just looked at Hansard, and I see that this reputable body of citizens-as after some inquiry I have found them to be-give some typical cases of relief there. They show, for example, that for two adults and seven children three to eighteen years of age the allowance on the relief work basis is $5.60 a week. For another family of two adults with two children ten and thirteen years of age the relief work schedule allows $3.50 a week. It seems to me that if those statements are correct, either the number of hours of work must be very few-and I do not think that is the case-or the rate of wages per hour
must be terribly low. If we have nothing in the nature of a fair wage clause, it seems to me that something should be done by our own department to check up the government of New Brunswick. That province, as I understand, is giving not direct relief but work relief; and if the conditions are as stated by this reputable body of citizens, careful supervision should be given of this particular situation in New Brunswick. I am not from New Brunswick, but I am a Canadian and I want to see that the people have at least an opportunity to live more decently than the schedule placed before us last night would seem to suggest. Is there any supervision at all?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Under the agreement with New Brunswick there is a clause providing that it shall be the responsibility of the province to see to it that all persons employed in the execution of works and undertakings are paid fair wages. Fair wages are the prevailing wages in the province in which the work is done, or rather the district, because sometimes there is a variation within the province.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Has the minister the schedule?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No. Normally, we would not have the schedule. It is exactly on the same basis as the relief scale established in the various provinces and in the various cities within the provinces. We do not ourselves control the relief scales nor do we control, except by this general clause, the actual wages paid on works within the province. I am not certain of the facts, but it may be that in New Brunswick the wages paid have conformed to the fair wage schedule within the province. I would assume that was so, otherwise it would be a violation of the agreement; but they may have worked for a comparatively small number of hours in order to reach the allowance mentioned by my hon. friend.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I was under the impression that the number of hours was given in the report last night, although I cannot find it in Hansard to-day. This is an agreement between the federal government and the provincial authorities. Could the federal government not see that the agreement is carried out? Could it not exercise some supervision? I suggest that at a subsequent time the minister might inform the committee what supervision has been exercised in Saint John, New Brunswick, what the schedules are, and what are the hours of work that give such a terribly low standard of living as that indicated in this particular report.
3042	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: On Monday last I placed on Hansard some figures with regard to the relief provided by Toronto for food. I also gave minimum figures as suggested by the Ontario Medical Association and the Cana-, dian Council on Nutrition, as well as League of Nations' figures. Taking the Ontario Medical Association and the council on nutrition, the relief paid in Toronto was shown to be 19 per cent lower than requirement. It is obvious from these figures that the scale of relief in that one particular city-and it is only illustrative-is too low, and that the food provided those on relief is not adequate, according to such authorities as I have quoted. If, in connection with wages, there is a general clause in the agreement providing that the province shall conform to a certain standard, could there not also be a general clause in regard to the food standards under which the agreement would operate? After all, if we are providing funds from the federal government to assist the provinces, and through the provinces the municipalities, surely we should have some say in regard to the standard to be provided under these agreements.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: On that point, the system of relief administration as it has developed in this country proceeds upon the principle that there is an immediate responsibility resting upon the municipalities with respect to relief scales. I know of no instance where the dominion government has declined to contribute to a particular scale on the ground that it was too high or too low. One must leave that with the authority that lies closest to the individuals concerned. We, at this distance, could not effectively supervise relief scales across the country. If you could adopt one scale across the entire country it might be a simple matter of administration, but my hon. friend will be the first to acknowledge that this could not be done. There must be some variation as between the city and the country, as between the city and the village, and as between province and province.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: But surely it is obvious that if a scale is 19 per cent below what is recognized by the Ontario Medical Association as the minimum, it is too low for that particular area. It does not make any difference whether a man's stomach receives nourishment in Montreal or Saint John or Toronto, In certain types of work there may be a variation in the number of calories required, certainly in the age group. But taking one city with another the standard should be essentially the same.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It seems to me that a report such as we had last jnight from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre

with regard to conditions in New Brunswick, calls for investigation. Chief Inspector Me-Leese of the police department of Saint John reported to the common council as follows:
Children have died this winter for no other reason in the world than that they were undernourished.
If we are bearing any part of the cost of this relief, and if we have an agreement and the wages paid are so pitifully low that the conditions outlined actually exist and children, according to this inspector, have died for no other reason in the world than that they were undernourished, then our department should take some responsibility and exercise supervision over the expenditure of funds.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I wish to associate myself most emphatically with t'he words of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). 'If there are municipalities in which the men in charge have so far got out of contact 'with human values that they are starving future Canadians to death, then it is high time that we instituted a publicity campaign to reveal to the rest of Canada what these people in' New Brunswick are doing, and to bring to the attention of these people in a vivid manner the fact that they are not discharging their responsibility to the Canada of to-morrow.

Section agreed to.
Progress reported.

It may surprise some hon. members of this committee to see me rise to speak on the question which has been raised by the hon. member for Peace River. But I had the privilege in 1933 of visiting the Peace River country and I know at least a little of the difficulties in the way of transportation which beset the citizens of that part of the country. In the session of 1934 I was one of those who seconded, while wTe were in opposition as the hon. member is now, the proposal for a Peace River outlet. The same difficulty existed then, that the public roads of the province are under the direct control of the province of Alberta. It was then considered
advisable to obtain from the province authorization for a contribution towards the building of the Peace River outlet. I am strongly in favour of the building of that road. I believe it is a necessity, very urgently required by the people in that part of the country. I do not know in just what way this or any other government might best proceed, but undoubtedly the Peace River district is one of the best sections of Canada. It is prosperous, the land is fertile, the people are industrious, and any government which undertook the building of that outlet would render a service not only to the people of the Peace River district but to the whole country. It would encourage people from the other provinces and from other countries to establish themselves in the Peace River district.
I must admit, however, that the argument of the minister is correct. While under the legislation a company or public body could obtain money, it is almost impossible for the federal government to interfere in provincial affairs, and public roads are undoubtedly under the direct control of the province. But I repeat, if this government can under any other circumstances assist in that project to help that part of the country, I should be one of those in eastern Canada to approve such action.

speechtext: I desire to thank the minister for the fairmindedness he has shown, and to thank also the hon. member for the Yukon and the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville. I feel sure that many members on both sides of the house would be glad to support such a project, because it is a matter of much more than local significance. speechtext:
All this week the house has been discussing Bill No. 96 and the resolution which preceded it. I am sure that no Liberal member can reasonably complain about the time the house has taken in dealing with these important questions of unemployment and agricultural distress; for I remember that between 1930 and 1935 we discussed the question of unemployment not for days but for weeks. I am sure that members of the Liberal party will display a little patience if for a short time I discuss this very important matter. Fortunately or unfortunately for myself, I was unable to be present during the preceding days of the week, but I carefully read Hansard and took note of what had been said. If there was one thing which impressed me in reading over the speeches, especially of the minister and those associated with him, it was the drifting attitude of the government and the totally ineffective methods they have adopted in the past few years to deal with this perplexing question.
I am sure that at this time no hon. member is more disappointed with the result of his efforts than the Minister of Labour himself. There has been no harder working minister of labour than the present one. No one, I believe, is more greatly respected by the mem-
[Mr. Rogers. 1
bers of the house than is the Minister of Labour. I feel sure that when he assumed office about three and a half years ago he did so in the high expectation that within a reasonable length of time the policies which the government would adopt would have some measure of effectiveness in so far as unemployment is concerned. But though the minister and those associated with him are anxious, I believe, that something of an effective nature should be done, unfortunately to-day we are no nearer the solution of the problem than we were when hon. gentlemen opposite assumed office. I recognize that the responsibility is not an easy one for any government to assume. But, in going through the speeches delivered during the past few days by the minister and others of his party, I find nothing of an effective nature in any proposals they intend to adopt during the brief lifetime that remains for the present government.
Another point which struck me forcibly was that, having practically admitted that they had no solution of the problem of unemployment, hon. members proceeded to throw jibes at the unemployed themselves. I am not blaming the Liberal party for that, but I do blame some hon. members because of the applause which evidently greeted certain remarks made on that side of the house. I do not think it is in the best interest of the unemployed themselves to sneer at them or call them insulting names because under existing conditions they are so unfortunate as not to have employment. From my personal observation of these young men I know that many of them are just as good as my own boys, as good as any boys we can find. What we are doing and have been doing for a number of years is enough to demoralize them, because we have not been able to make out of them the useful citizens they should be.

speechtext: The amendment was proposed a moment ago and has been read aloud to the committee. The purpose of that amendment is to permit the passing of an order in council which would authorize a loan for relief purposes covering a province's share of relief expenditures made in the dominion's preceding fiscal year. Due to some of the western provinces' fiscal years ending April 30, a month later than the close of the dominion's fiscal year, and due to the uncertainty as to what the provinces' share of the unemployment relief costs will be, for some time after the close of their fiscal years, it is deemed advisable to provide this authority to make any loan which may be found necessary to cover the provinces' relief outlays during the fiscal year 1938-39. speechtext: However, the ruling has been given, and I do not want to transgress. But may I just say this. The section provides for the granting of financial assistance to the provinces by way of loans, advances or guarantees for the purpose of assisting the province to pay its share of expenditures incurred for the purposes mentioned in section 4 of the act. I wish to draw to the attention of the minister again a situation that is right under our noses in this particular city. There are as a matter of fact about a hundred men in this city at the present time who are without a place to sleep in. These men find it impossible to obtain relief from the authorities because they cannot establish domicile- exactly what we were discussing a day or two ago. I understand that these facts have been presented both to the mayor of the city and to the Hon. Eric Cross, but nothing has been done. To my personal knowledge some of these men are ill, and owing to the fact that they are living under these conditions more of them are likely to become ill. It seems to me that when we are discussing a section of this kind we should impress upon the minister the necessity of assuming an obligation to persuade, if I may put it that way, the provincial or the local authorities to do something to alleviate this distress.

I want every man to be happy and just as prosperous as a man can be in this country. That is my earnest hope. I do not see why men who are my countrymen, good sturdy people, should be deprived of opportunity to earn their living decently, on account of some trouble which is not theirs. Before the subject is closed may I say it is quite evident from the applause that members of the committee do not clearly understand the nature of the existing legislation in its relationship to the provinces. Of course no one can quarrel with what the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) advocates with respect to citizens of the province of Quebec, and of the constituency of Temiscouata in particular, who are suffering under adverse conditions. The question is rather one of method, depending upon where the distress occurs.
The test under this legislation as to the eligibility of a province for a loan is, first, its demonstrated inability to take care of its own share of the expenditure under consideration. That is to say, there is first the province's share of direct relief. The test there is: Are the province's own resources at this time, as revealed by financial statements which from month to month they must submit to the minister, adequate to meet their own share of the expenditure? Sometimes they are in part adequate, in which case they do not get a loan for the full amount. In some cases they are quite inadequate, in which case they get a loan up to the amount of their own share of the expenditure on direct relief.
The next question is this. All the various cooperative schemes which are in effect as between the dominion and the provinces for providing works of various kinds under various departments of the government in each case involve a provincial share. That is, the province must be prepared to spend some of its own money. In that case also, only if a province demonstrates that its own revenues prevent it from going into the scheme without the aid of a loan from the dominion is a loan made.
Coming to the specific matter mentioned by the hon. member for Temiscouata, within the scope of existing legislation resettlement schemes are operating cooperatively as between the dominion and any province desiring to enter into such an arrangement. The dominion contributes; the province contributes; also in some cases the municipalities contribute-I believe that is under the Department of Agriculture, is it not?

In that connection of course I need not tell the hon. member for Temiscouata we have never had an application from Quebec based upon the essential principle that the province was unable to meet its own share.
Under this legislation we have power to enter into resettlement arrangements. One of the ministers concerned with resettlement more intimately than I am could deal with that phase of the matter. The official before me tells me that most resettlement schemes are provincial in character, and do not necessarily come under cooperative undertakings. But it does run in my mind that in connection with some provinces there is and has been a measure of cooperation by the federal government in connection with resettlement. Therefore I was entirely in sympathy with what the Minister of Finance said regarding a resettlement scheme. It would seem that when Canada was settled there was no planned idea in respect to the manner in which the people should settle. It is time now that the provinces, the municipalities and the dominion got together for the good of the people and proposed some planned scheme of settlement whereby those people could make a living.
I realize that many of the people in Temiscouata who live on their own land, and children moving from their homes into the immediate neighbourhood, have settled on land on which it is very difficult indeed to make a living.
