Looking about the chamber I see that there are only a couple of Liberal members from Saskatchewan now present. If there were more of them here,
I know they would smile when I make the statement that I am going to try to do something on behalf of that government. It is reported in the western press that Hon. A. T. Proctor, provincial minister of highways, is en route to Ottawa to seek federal assistance for an extensive road program. The report states that the premier and the attorney general are with him, and it goes on to say:
Except for the ordinary expenditures f<pr highway maintenance, no money was voted in the legislature for highways construction this year. Consequently the only road construction undertaken will be whatever the province can obtain assistance for in Ottawa.
I trust that when this appeal is made tc the minister he will give it every consideration. The highways of the province are not in good shape. This report states that the provincial minister is going to make a special appeal in connection with the highways running north and south from the United States boundary to highway No. 1. About 140 miles of that highway running west from the Manitoba boundary must be covered before you reach hard surface. The importance of the hard surfacing of our highways was discussed last evening, and I was sorry more hon. members from the west were not here to support the proposal made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I am glad to have that information, because comment is often made in this house on the amount of money the government is lending the west. Given ordinary conditions in western Canada, I am satisfied that the people of the western provinces would be only too happy to pay back every single dollar lent to them by the federal treasury, and that up to date they have paid the interest charges on their loans is an indication of that very fact.
There is one thing I wish to say to hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not see why they should be so anxious to call out at every opportunity "carried"-"carried"-"carried." I remember when some of them were in this chamber in 1930 and in 1935, and the long weeks that were taken in discussing this very same kind of legislation. We have been discussing the legislation now before us for only a comparatively short time, and hon. gentlemen opposite seem anxious not to allow it to be discussed in the way it ought to be discussed. If hon. members who apparently do not wish to discuss this measure would allow others who do wish to discuss it the opportunity to do so, there would be no harm done. In discussing the legislation hon. members are only exercising a right which is theirs as members of this house. It may be that some members are on their feet a little too often but no one can accuse me of that, because this is the first afternoon I have said a word on this legislation. I have been absent through no fault of my own.
This question of unemployment is one tihat seriously affects our constituencies, and it is of particular importance to my own constituency. I am not going to discuss it now at any length, but I do wish to make a mild protest against some hon. members opposite attempting to dispose summarily of what is after all the most important question that confronts the house at the present time. Not only that, but if they will turn their minds back to 1930 and think of all the things they said about unemployment during the election campaign of that year, they will realize how much it helped them to obtain the seats they now occupy in this chamber. On the third reading of the bill I shall make some extended remarks. All I wish to say now is that hon. members opposite should not interrupt those who desire to speak on this legislation, which is of great importance to some of us.

speechtext:
The other evening I was about to ask the minister if he would explain the present situation in British Columbia with regard to forestry project camps. I should like a further word of explanation also in order that we may distinguish between the two types of camps. I understand the one type is expressly for training purposes in the summer, while the type of camp operated in the winter months is for transients and those in destitute circumstances. Also I should like to know when they are likely to close this year.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS: (Minister of Labour):	Forestry conservation
camps operated in winter in British Columbia are intended to provide for single unemployed men, largely in the cities of the province. The camps usually begin to operate in October and continue until April or May. Provision is made for the deferring of a portion of the payments to those who work in these camps in order that they may have some means at their disposal when they leave in the spring. The forestry training camps operate in the summer, usually beginning in May. It is intended rather to bring into those camps men of a fixed age group, young men of eighteen to twenty-five, who receive training while they are also doing certain conservation work such as the construction of fire trails.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Wihat is the present
position of the eastern transients? Will they all be sent back east under whatever circumstances, or have they been allowed to secure in some instances the cash they have earned at destinations other than those indicated on the interrogation form?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Those who came from
eastern points and therefore were not accepted by British Columbia as its responsibility were permitted to go into the camps until such time as they would earn an amount sufficient to pay their transportation back to the point from which they came. Apart from the Cultus Lake camp-

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Was there not another?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
There was another at Capilano, and my understanding is that the
Supply-Labour

men in that camp are working out their transportation under the plan originally proposed, or have already done so.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Some of these men when interviewed last fall indicated that they had hopes of employment at points other than those indicated on the interrogation form when they were admitted to the camp. speechtext: The arrangement was, and it was one to which they consented, that they should receive transportation back to the point in eastern Canada that they indicated. The understanding was that they should receive transportation back to the points which they themselves indicated before they entered the camp.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

that pays the shot for most of that work out there, and-

speechtext: Does the minister appreciate the fact that the authorities in the cities are disturbed as to the prospect of the release of a large number of men from these camps? speechtext:
I am sure the provincial
department of labour has that situation in hand. My understanding is that the time of the closing of the camps has been extended beyond last year's closing time, and the belief is that when the camps are closed there will be sufficient volume of employment available.

Supply-Labour

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Did the minister get
the number of rejections?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I explained to the hon.
member for Weyburn that we will have to get that information from Saskatchewan. It is not yet available.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: When the minister gives these figures I presume they include men who worked for a week or a month, or some other short time?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: They include the total number of placements. The great majority of them remained for a period of months.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: That is, they would be on a farm three or four months, or whatever the length of time may be, and then when the work was finished they would drift and wander around for another year. Then they may go back to the farm. That is perhaps one of the saddest features of the whole situation. Young men who are maturing, at the ages of twenty-five or thirty years work on the farms and receive in the neighbourhood of $10 a month -and I do not think I am understating it when I name that amount. In fact, an hon. member to my left tells me I may be overstating it. However, if they received $10 a month it would not present much of a future for them. All we do for the young man in Canada is to provide him with a job on a farm at $10 a month, barely sufficient to take care of the necessities of life, besides food and shelter. Can the government not do better in that respect than it has been doing, in order to give those young men a little more than they have received in years gone by? I think the government's contribution has been $5 a month.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: It has been $7.50, if they remained.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I do not know what additional sums they may have received from the farmers, but in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta, where the farmers have had such a bad time of it in the past few years, I am certain that in many cases the farmer would find it extremely difficult to supplement the amount received from the government. I am not thinking of the immediate present so far as these men are concerned. I am trying to look a little ahead, possibly a year or two years, to see if we cannot get something which would present more of an incentive than is presented by this procedure of putting a man on a farm at $7.50 or $10 a month. Certainly in a country such as Canada, rich in natural resources and in other respects, we ought to do better than that.
We ought to be able to do more than to give our young men $7.50 a month when we send them to work on the farms.
As has been said just now and on previous occasions by the minister, these young men prefer to accept that amount, rather than go on the dole or do nothing. I believe great credit is due them for that spirit. They prefer work to public relief. But when they do work they should be given some encouragement, and should not be working for such a small amount. If a young man worked four months on a farm he would leave the farm with about $30. He would require clothes and other essentials of life, and I think that amount is very little for a man who has devoted four months of his time working on a farm helping to gather in the nation's wealth. Would it be such a heavy burden on the national treasury if the government were to supplement the $7.50 and make it $10 a month, so that work on the farm would be a little more attractive?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I returned yesterday from the Pacific coast, where I learned-and the minister will correct me if I am wrong-that there were about 4,000 single unemployed in the forestry camps throughout the winter, and that all those men will be out of the camps and their deferred pay will have run out by June 1. Am I correct in that?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Yes, that is correct.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
There is considerable apprehension at the coast as to what will happen after June 1, and I suggest that some provision be made for the men after the closing of the camps, or after their money has run out. I was told the policy of the government seemed to be one of feeding the men through the winter, but doing nothing or very little to help establish them in work in the summer. I learned from reliable authorities that about sixty-five per cent of the men in the camps this year were repeaters. No doubt the minister will be able to inform the committee as to the accuracy of that information. If it is correct, it is an indication of the seriousness of the situation. The suggestion was made that it might be worth while for the government, working through a business men's committee, to establish a farming training unit on an experimental basis, and also some unit for training in mining, forestry and road building. The expense need not be very great. There is a citizens' committee in Vancouver, known as the citizens' recreational council, which is doing splendid work under the provincial government. I ask the minister to consider carefully trying out such a scheme as I have suggested. If a farm
Supply-Labour

were taken over in order to give some of these young men training, eventually it might be used as a home for older men admittedly unemployable. We might be able to build up some system which would help solve this problem which is worrying us all, and probably the minister more than anyone else.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The provincial department of labour has maintained close contact with the welfare organizations in Vancouver, and I would assume also with this citizens' committee to which my hon. friend has referred.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: It is under the provincial government.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I feel sure that every precaution is being taken in closing these camps to see that the men are assisted toward employment. This does not mean that the only employment to which they will be assisted will be that provided by the various governments. I understand that the logging companies in British Columbia are in a somewhat better position this summer to provide employment. A year ago the amount of employment provided was far short of what it was thought it would be possible to provide.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I was told that a farming training unit would need an expenditure of only $10,000, but apparently the province cannot put up the money. I suggest it might be worth while for the dominion to try something on a small scale. Even if the money were lost, it would not be such a large amount, and if the scheme proved successful it might give a lead toward settling the whole question.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). Surely it is worth all the trouble in the world to see that some suitable action is taken at this time to prevent trouble in the future. We have had this problem presented to us in its most aggravated form in British Columbia over and over again. I do not want to be critical, I simply want to offer constructive suggestions. Would it not be possible for the employment service of Canada to undertake special activities in connection with the men about to be released from the camps? Could there not be something worked out in the way of a vocational guidance? Or perhaps special examinations could be held to discover the special aptitude or experience of the men. The experience in the past has been that as these men are released from the camps they drift back to the various centres when they begin to wander. They cannot plan or finance their wanderings, and they become a charge upon the community. The charitable agencies

sometimes find themselves unable to deal with the problem, and the men start out panhandling and riding the rods here and there in any direction in which they think there will be some form of work. The information that they get on their own initiative is generally most unsatisfactory, and the result is that quite often they become destitute in their wanderings. I do hope that we may have a word from the minister that some special activity will be carried on through the employment service in an effort to exhaust every last hope of employment for these men.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend that it would be desirable that some special effort be made by the employment service of' Canada, and I shall take whatever action I can to see that this is done. My hon. friend is aware that under the existing arrangement this is a matter which would require cooperative action by the two governments.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I am really disturbed about the condition of our young people. The farm placement scheme assisted to some extent, but after all it was an emergency measure. Some thousands were placed under that scheme this winter in the province from which I come, but all they are getting is $5 a month, with an additional $2.50 if they remain the whole period. The regulations are such that a farmer's son or daughter living in a home where there is no future is debarred from obtaining even this pittance. I do not know what is to be done. My personal contacts with many of these young people lead me to believe that their condition is really a major tragedy. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) referred to the rise in illegitimacy figures. This is one phase of the matter, but another phase is the fact that these people are getting soured by the conditions under which they have to live. If they go on like this for a number of years I am afraid of the ultimate outcome. I realize that with the huge expenditures required, it is quite difficult for the government to consider any broadening of the scheme, but something will have to be done to bring more of these young people under the scheme. We will have to give them something more to which to look forward.
The amount paid should be increased so that a young man may be able to dress decently. I realize the difficulties the minister has to face, and I know that much of what he has done in connection with youth training has been good. I think it is a departure that has been welcomed. A short time ago I was glad to be able to pass along to the minister an appreciation which I had

Supply-Labour
received from one of the towns in my constituency. The people there felt that this was a step in the right direction. However, to deal with this question we must go far beyond the point we have now reached. I endeavoured to ask a question earlier this afternoon, but apparently in doing so I transgressed the rules. I have in my hand a publication issued by the Department of Labour dealing with the training of Canada's young unemployed. There is a table of figures on page 24, and I should like to have some explanation of these figures from the minister. I do not quite follow them. If possible I should like to have this table put on Hansard.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Those figures are over a year old. I intend to place more up to date figures on Hansard in the course of a few days when the youth training bill is before the house.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Then I shall wait.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Would the minister explain the -basis under which men are admitted to these training projects in connection with mining and forestry? Is admittance limited to persons living in homes where material aid is being given, or does it apply also to persons living in homes in the lower income brackets?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: It is not limited entirely to those receiving material aid. It is intended to cover those in necessitous circumstances who may not be actually on relief.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Is there any specific quota? There has been great difficulty in filling the needs of the young people in the suburban areas who would like to get some training.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: It was not thought possible to establish a quota which would be satisfactory right across Canada. Naturally we felt that those who came from families on relief should have priority.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: What is the significance of the phrase "supplementary plans"? What -has the minister in view?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: That is placed here to give us some freedom to undertake alternative plans other than farm employment and forest conservation in dealing with single unemployed men.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Would that not come under Bill No. 94?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: No, under this item.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I have 'been informed that a number of single unemployed men in the city of Ottawa have been transferred during the last few days to camps at Trenton, Petawawa and Borden. What kind of camps are these? What will the men be doing in them? Do they come under this vote?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I did make inquiries myself in the course of the last few days at the employment office as to the employment made available through that office during the past two weeks. My understanding is that some men have 'been offered employment at Petawawa. The actual work is, I believe, being done iby the Department of National Defence. It is the removal of -brush and so forth from the ranges, under the supervision, I understand, of the forestry station at Petawawa. I do not know as to the work to which my hon. friend referred at Borden and Trenton.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Have any steps been taken to set up in Canada a farm hostel plan, particularly for the older men? The publication of the Canadian welfare council entitled "Wayfarers Perforce," says at page 36:
It appears that the older migrant, if given any opportunity whatever, is ready and anxious to become fixed in his abode. For that reason it is thought that the farm hostel plan might provide for the definitely unemployable group. As yet there is not sufficient information available as to the measure of success achieved by this plan, which has been in operation in a few communities, but it would seem that some such method might be suitable.
The report goes on to set out that the hostels would be fairly close to the larger centres and that older men with like interests, miners for instance, and others engaged in different occupations, could be organized into congenial groups and placed in the hostels. It also points out that eventually the provinces might be willing to recognize these hostels as part of their charitable institution program and provide them with grants or, alternatively, maintenance costs. Has anything along that line been done by the federal government, and if not, could not something of that kind be done?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Another vote deals with the rehabilitation of older unemployed persons. It is possible for the provinces to submit a plan of that kind to us for approval under this vote. As a matter of fact, in three provinces, although perhaps the plan is not the farm hostel plan, progress has been made in establishing groups of the older unemployed in farming operations.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
In what provinces?
Supply-Labour

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: In Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I would direct the minister's attention to the fact that in some of the camps maintained under this vote there are ex-service men. Would he approve the suggestion that steps be taken in cooperation with the Department of Pensions and National Health that when ex-service men go into these camps they be automatically checked up as to their rights under the war veterans' allowance and pension acts and medical treatment regulations so that they can get the utmost opportunity to secure rehabilitation? It is distressing that there Should be so many exservice men in these camps. May I also ask *whether it is possible for the minister in cooperation with the Department of Pensions and National Health, to deal in some other way with ex-service men, particularly in regard to medical treatment?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
In connection with the
camps in British Columbia, which are the ones now in operation, we received a request from Colonel Foster of the Canadian Legion that men with war service who were eligible for the camps should be placed in separate camps. That has been done, and, I believe, with complete success. We also secured the cooperation of the Canadian Legion in obtaining men who are giving physical training and recreational direction in the camps. The suggestion of my hon. friend is a good one, and I will bring it to the attention of my colleague.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The minister stated that single homeless unemployed in Ottawa were being given work at Petawawa, Trenton and Rockeliffe.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Petawawa only.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Surely the minister is not leaving these men to the tender mencies of the Department of National Defence, is he?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: It is simply the work that is ordinarily done in order to put the camp in order for artillery manoeuvres in the summer months. The men are receiving the regular prevailing wage, at an hourly rate. Whether or not they are being accommodated in tents or. the property at Petawawa I am not in a position to say, but they are receiving the normal hourly rate.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
They are not in the
national defence camps, are they? That is what I wanted to make sure of.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: No, they are not.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Facing the fact that the Cowichan river is eroding its banks, can relief be obtained under this vote and men put to work to do what is necessary?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I think a project of that land would more properly come under the general vote, which we shall shortly reach.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: What training schemes have been adopted for the middle-aged group of unemployed? The minister said last year that some schemes would be adopted for them.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: We have not yet reached that vote. I have no desire to avoid discussion of the question except that there will shortly be before the house a bill dealing with youth training projects, and I would suggest that rather than duplicate the discussion, the bill would be a more suitable time to consider various youth training projects.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: And this will be the first year's vote for projects under that bill?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
If I am not in order in
bringing this matter up under this vote, I shall bring it up later, but I have been asked to bring it to the minister's attention. I understand that some of the students engaged under the youth training plan are doing actual practical work as electricians, or in other trades. They are doing work that is ordinarily done by men in the various trades, who receive employment thereby. But that is not the issue. I would ask whether the government receives any remunation from such work. I am informed that some work is being done on city property. I think it is good thing that young people should have a practical training along that line, but would the city receive the financial benefit of such work, or would the city repay to this government the cost of it?

Supply-Labour

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I would assume that there
would be no return to the governments concerned. I might say that any projects of that kind undertaken in Alberta have been submitted to this government by the provincial government; knowing the way in which these projects have been administered, I feel quite sure that every care has been taken to prevent any abuse, and I would assume, on the facts, stated by my hon. friend, that the work was done for training purposes only.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I do not wish to be misunderstood. I said I had been asked to present this question. It was not the Alberta government that asked me to present it. I was asked by a number of youths who were working on a certain project, because they felt that if some contractor had the job of putting in the electrical equipment, and thereby receive payment, perhaps they themselves, being up against it, might receive some little remuneration for their work.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I will take note of the question, and if there is any further information I shall place it before my hon. friend.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I do not quite follow
what this rehabilitation work consists of.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: We are not yet actually on that item. We are on item 509.

Item agreed to.
510.	To provide, in cooperation with the provinces, for rehabilitation of unemployed persons, $680,000.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Will the minister now answer my question?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
This deals also with the question raised by the hon. member for Yale. Last year this item was inserted for the first
time. I wished to apply rehabilitation projects to the older unemployed persons. It was an experimental vote. As soon as the vote became available, letters were sent to all provincial governments informing them that a certain portion of this vote was made available to them and asking them to submit what they thought would be suitable projects within their own province for the relief of older unemployed persons. The response was not as general as it had been in connection with youth training. One reason given was that the rehabilitation of older unemployed persons presented far greater problems, that it was not possible to get the same degree of cooperation, for example from labour bodies and from voluntary organizations. But I can say that, even in some provinces which have not yet proposed schemes, we believe that schemes are now being developed and that they will be put in operation during the present fiscal year.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
What sort of plan is
contemplated?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Well, in Alberta and Ontario proposals have been put forward for placing some of these older unemployed men on very small holdings in the neighbourhood of cities in order that such men might engage in market gardening under supervision. That is being done in an experimental way in those two provinces. In Manitoba a number of men have been placed on farms under what is known as the farm chore plan, and a number also have been given reconditioning work and some training in the White Shell forest reserve. I am not able to say to the committee that the work thus far has been on a large scale. As I have said, the plans have to be developed by the provinces concerned.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Is there anything from British Columbia?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: We have had no plan from British Columbia. I believe it is likely that plans will be submitted this year.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Are any schemes of a different type in contemplation for the coming year?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Perhaps I should have
added that in Manitoba quite a number of these older unemployed men have been taught to make rustic furniture. That has been done in connection with work in the White Shell forest reserve. I myself have seen some of the work; there was an exhibition of it at the provincial buildings in Winnipeg. It was excellent work; whether it will prove commercially profitable is another question. But
Supply-Labour

our purpose is to take these older men from the hostels and place them in more advantageous surroundings, to teach them something which would enable them to support themselves entirely or conduce towards that end.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Has the minister any idea of the extent of the problem, the numbers that would fall into these several categories? Has he any idea of. the number of men in this drifter category between, we will say, forty and fifty, or thirty and forty? Have we really any data on which we can go?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: All we would have would be the number of those on relief within that age group, and also the number of that age group in the various hostels.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: So that really so far we have not a comprehensive view of the whole problem?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Well, I would suggest to my hon. friend that certainly the greatest need would be revealed by the figures of those within those age categories who are on relief. I say, the greatest need; I do not say, the only ones in need.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: While we are discussing the matter of rehabilitation, which becomes increasingly necessary at this time, has the minister or the department any suggestions for a committee on social research or something of that kind? It must be becoming increasingly clear to the minister himself that, while we have available all the means to produce and distribute goods, there is something which enters in between the material things and the people who require them. Has he given any thought to the idea of setting up a committee on social research to explore ways which up to now have not been tried which would enable the people of this dominion through their cooperative effort to become self-sustaining?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: We have, of course, the benefit of such studies as have been made independently upon this question. There is also the experience of other countries with the same problem. What is perhaps even more valuable, we have the experience of the provincial governments themselves who are continually face to face with this question of transferring one group of the population from one occupation to another. I doubt if any additional committee of social research workers could throw any more light upon the problem itself than is now available.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Would it not help both the federal and the provincial governments if honorary advisory committees were set up

in each province to make suggestions with regard to these different plans, not only in regard to youth but for the rehabilitation of the middle-aged group? This government relies too much on suggestions from provincial governments. They are all hard-pressed and have not much time to think up new schemes, and I submit that no government can get the human slant on a problem as well as a group of individuals can. Would it not be possible to set up honorary advisory committees in the various part of Canada, perhaps more than one in each province? I am afraid the governments have reached the stage where they have stopped experimenting because they are holding the fort, so to speak, and are not looking round for remedies.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: We have honorary advisory committees set up in most of the provinces in connection with the youth training program, and we have also a small national advisory committee, which I hope will be broadened shortly, now that we are able to put youth training on a three-year training program. There was great difficulty in arousing interest in youth training plans when they were on an annual basis. I quite agree that there might be an advantage in having such committees act in connection with these rehabilitation plans. Some of the plans now in operation in Manitoba have been greatly assisted by these committees.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Business people and citizens in all walks of life in each community are only too anxious to get at the problem. Honorary advisory committees worked well under the home improvement plan; they might also be tried in connection with the employment agencies; we might get some valuable suggestions with regard to the employment service.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Is the Department of Labour making any effort to get complete-registration of those unemployed as distinct from those actually on relief?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend's question comes under item fill.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I should like to get some information with regard to small holdings. How successful has that scheme been; what does the scheme comprise; how much assistance is given the settler after he has settled on the land, and so on? Is the scheme carried on for a number of years?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: What percentage of failures has there been?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The number of abandonments was given in the previous discussion. There are about 20 per cent of abandonments in that type of settlement. The other plan is more recent, and we have not enough experience to say whether it will prove successful, but the government of Alberta presented to us not long ago a plan whereby some families could be placed on small holdings near the larger cities.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: That is a smaller scheme.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Are we to understand definitely that the individual provinces have to initiate the scheme if they wish to get assistance?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: What we have done in youth training and in connection with the rehabilitation of older unemployed persons is to indicate broadly the type of project which we should like to have submitted, and in doing so we follow the recommendations of the national employment commission. Then we ask the province to decide, with its more accurate knowledge of the possibilities of reestablishment, what projects are most likely to succeed.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: This problem of the rehabilitation of unemployed persons is to a large extent, although not wholly, of course, a problem of the transients.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I agree.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: As was revealed in the discussion, a great many of these men cannot establish residence anywhere. The weakness of this whole rehabilitation plan is that it is provincial. To my mind we are getting closer and closer to the point where we must assume direct responsibility federally for some of these matters, and this is an activity that ought to be regarded as a national problem. I am sorry to hear that this experimental vote has not been taken advantage of to a greater extent than it has been, but the vote is well worth while, and I should like to see consideration given to at least this phase of the unemployment problem with a view to bringing it directly under the federal department.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The minister said that he intended to set up another committee. Would that be similar to the committee set up under the Purvis commission?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: What I had in mind was that there would be provincial advisory committees which would assist both in directing the governments concerned to suitable projects of youth training and, later, in the placement of those who had received training. In so far as the national advisory committee is concerned, that will consist of representatives from the various interests, who would most probably assist the government in its broader program of youth training.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Would there be one set up in each province?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The hon. member's colleague from Vancouver South (Mr. Green) made that suggestion, and I told him that in some provinces these committees were set up on a wholly voluntary basis. I emphasize that. If there is to be a broadening of the national advisory committee, as I hope there will be, it will be on a voluntary basis.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: That is what I had in mind.

Youth training, $60,000.
Comptroller of the treasury's office for field examination of accounts under relief legislation, $100,000.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Does any part of this go to the province?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: This covers the staff of the unemployment relief branch of the federal Department of Labour.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Does the same apply to the $60,000 for youth training?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Is any attempt made to register the actual number of persons unemployed as distinct from those actually on relief?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
As perhaps my hon. friend is aware, we have discussed that question here previously. In the United States, an attempt was made, under the direction, I think, of the president of the American Rolling Mills, to take what was called a census of unemployment. It was done in cooperation with the Post Office Department; it was organized as
Supply-Labour

efficiently as could be under the circumstances; but when all the figures were in, the director admitted that he did not know whether the figures as assembled were within 1,500,000 or 2,000,000 of the actual total. In other words, from the time the study was commenced to the time the figures were in and assembled there had been a vast change in the unemployment situation in the United States. That is the great difficulty in a situation of that kind.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: That was probably the most important part of the work which was supposed to be done by the national employment commission.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Well, the commission
reached the same conclusion.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Then we have reached the conclusion that it is next to impossible to get definite figures as to the number of unemployed at any time?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
We might require under
penalty that every one who was unemployed should report, say at a post office, on a certain day. But there is no reason to believe that even that would provide us with more than a knowledge of the situation on that particular day. One would need some kind of continuous machinery in order to get the continuous trends. In England they get their figures through the unemployment insurance. If we had a national system of unemployment insurance we would get these figures as far as insured groups are concerned. The English figures are most accurate because their insurable groups cover a large proportion of the working population.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Then the nearest information as to the actual number of unemployed is the figures furnished by the bureau of statistics?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Yes, which, as my hon.
friend knows, are always put forward as an estimate.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

speechtext: Practically all of it.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Under this item I should like to say a few words which I would have said before six o'clock, had there been time or a proper opportunity to do so. In all the years I have been in the house I do not believe I have ever seen an estimate reduced in amount, nor has there been any invitation by any minister at any time to reduce one. I do not know how estimates are made up. However, here is a large item amounting to more than $3,000,000, an amount about $300,000 greater than last year. It is an item which appears in the estimates every year, always more or less the same size, to pay for the dredging at Montreal.
When Premier Hepburn recently introduced his estimates into the Ontario legislature he immediately invited hon. members in some way to cut them down. Is it out of the question to have anything like that in this house? This is my tenth session, and I have never yet been asked, either by this government or the previous one-yes, I used to protest to them, too, about not being able to change estimates-to change an amount. That seems to me ridiculous. Here we are, considering an estimate, but we cannot change it one dollar, because the minister will see to it that it goes through in its present form, and he has the majority behind him to put it through.
If what the premier of Ontario has proposed to cut down expenses of administration is good, then it might be a good plan to try it here. I do not know how these estimates are made up, but, as I began to say before six o'clock, in the old country a committee of all parties consisting of twenty-eight members of parliament survey the estimates and they change them, as I understand. I may be wrong, but that is the way in which I interpret the book I read on the subject. Nothing like that is done in this house. It is all one-sided. Whichever party is in power brings in the estimates, and they have to go through in that form.
In the United States they have what I believe is called a budget committee, made up of members of the two main parties, the Republicans and the Democrats. I inquired carefully into that fact while I was in Washington, and that was the information I got. The information given me may not have been correct, but that is what I was told. In that committee they discuss the items before they are brought into the chamber.
Sup-ply-Transport-M arine

If that sort of procedure will cut down costs of administration, then I say we ought to begin doing it in this house. Certainly every year the cost of administration is up, up, up, up, up-never down. Never at any time in the ten years I have been in the house do I remember the cutting down of an estimate. Is it against the law of the land to cut down an estimate? It would appear to me that it must be. There is nothing we can say about an estimate which would change it. But, if a committee consisting of Liberals, Conservatives, Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members, and members of the Social Credit party quietly looked over these estimates while sitting round a table, they could decide whether or not this one should go up or that one should go down.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: They should go to a committee.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I am trying to show that anything we do in committee of the whole cannot change an estimate one iota. I have never seen them changed while I have been here.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: They might be, if they went to a committee.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: If we followed the plan which is adopted elsewhere we would bring the estimates to the house after they had been surveyed, and after the decision had been made as to whether the expenditures were really necessary. Any pork-barrel item could be wiped out-but not in this house. Every item goes through here.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member is misinformed as to the practice elsewhere. It is my understanding that under the British form of responsible government the government of the day must take full responsibility for the amount of supply it asks the House of Commons to vote. More often than not it has been my experience in the House of Commons that members of other parties have asked the minister to increase votes-

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I am asking the minister to cut them.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: We have had ten speeches urging an increase of votes to one urging reductions. Does my hon. friend suggest that a minister should permit any member of the house to increase a vote the minister brings down? If that were so, how would the Minister of Finance be able to prepare a budget?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The minister does not understand me.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Yes, I understand fully. The hon. member thinks this particular vote should be reduced.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: No, I did not confine my comment to this vote.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: There is no British practice which permits any committee of the House of Commons to change an estimate introduced into the house. It is considered that the responsible minister has studied the matter thoroughly, with the assistance of all the resources of his department. The government stands or falls on being able to have passed the estimates it brings to this house. I think that is the practice in Great Britain just as it is here.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I have told the minister that is not the practice.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Instead of the estimates being referred to a committee of the whole house in Great Britain, it is quite true they are referred to a select committee, just as in Canada the estimates affecting railway expenditures are referred to a select committee of this house. But it has never been my understanding that it was the privilege of a select committee in Great Britain to change the amount of an estimate brought down by a responsible minister.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I did not refer to changing them after they are brought down. I was referring to considering them before they are brought down. The committee in Great Britain is called the select committee on estimates, and I understand it is made up of members from the different parties. They sit round a table and consider the estimates before they are brought into the house. May be I misunderstood the account.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: No. In Great Britain, the select committee which examines the estimates is analogous to a committee of the whole house that examines the estimates here. These estimates are not prepared as the result of any one man's judgment. They are considered by the cabinet as a whole and by committees of the cabinet. A tremendous amount of study is given to these estimates. Once they are brought into the house, whether they are to be considered by a select committee, as in England, or by a committee of the whole house, as here, the practice is exactly the same.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
When estimates are brought before a committee of the whole house the discussion is more or less formal, but if they were brought before a special committee we could go into them in detail in a way that

Suppl y- Transport-M arine
we cannot here. As the minister knows, in connection with the Canadian National Railways estimates the officers of the railway are present and then is given to hon. members information which it is impossible to give in committee of the whole. I feel quite sure that if some of these estimates, not necessarily the one we are discussing, could be sent to a special committee, hon. members would be able to obtain a much more intelligent understanding of the work of the departments. Such a procedure would mean less discussion in committee of the whole, but certainly more discussion in the special committee. There would appear before that committee experts from the various departments who had had a hand in preparing the estimates. I do not know very much about this particular vote; if it were SI,000,000 or $10,000.000, I would not be any the wiser, except for what little the minister might divulge to the committee. I do not think it is an intelligent way to pass such huge appropriations of money when no one in the committee, outside the minister and the officials who are present, can possibly know anything about the items.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I am in accord with what has been said about the method of dealing with estimates. I think it would be much better if the members could be better informed before these items were passed. I notice that over $400,000 more is being asked for contract dredging, and I should like to know why it is necessary to increase this vote.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The department is engaged
on a program of deepening the St. Lawrence river channel to thirty-five feet over a definite period of years. An interdepartmental committee was set up to study this matter, and a large amount was appropriated to cover the cost of studying the development of the St. Lawrence. That committee reported on a program to complete the channel at a cost of about 811,500,000. This government decided that the economical way to do this work was by contract rather than to continue to use inadequate and obsolete equipment owned by the government. Under the arrangements by which this equipment was sold we gave the purchasers of it an estimate that this work would be carried on at the rate of approximately $3,000,000 a year. The amount spent in the last two years fell below this estimate, last year $2,933,000 being spent on contract dredging and a somewhat smaller sum the year before. This year we decided that we would get back to the agreed program, and
the amount that this is above the $3,000,000 is the amount that we have fallen behind in previous years. It is intended to bring the work back to the schedule of $3,000,000 a year.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Is that much more work going to be done?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Certainly. This program
is within the program laid down by the committee. My hon. friend knows a good deal about that committee because it functioned in his day, and I know he takes a great interest in this type of work. We are following the recommendations of that committee as to the work to be done, and the program being followed will bring about the completion of the deep water channel in 1943.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
How many contractors
were there, and how many contracts does this represent?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: There is just the one contract, but there are several contractors.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Did they all bid?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I believe this contract was
entered into in 1930. It was open to competitive tender and was awarded to the lowest tenderer of that day. It was extended twice by the previous government and once by this government. A contract of this size attracts all the suitable plant in the country. One could not hope to have real competition for a job which requires plant of a certain class and which represents about all the plant of that class in Canada. The last contract was negotiated at the time of the sale of our equipment. In many instances we have lowered the unit price, and in no instance has the unit price been increased over the price which prevailed during the previous five years.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: As I understand it, the ultimate object is to deepen the St. Lawrence river channel from Montreal to the sea to a depth of thirty-five feet, in order to allow practically any vessel to come to Montreal.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Yes, that is the object.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Not any boat.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The Empress of Britain draws thirty-three feet, and she would hardly come up a thirty-five foot channel because the margin would be too small. She might get up to Montreal by watching the tides carefully, but I do not think this deepening will permit the Empress of Britain to come to that city.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I find myself in complete accord with what hon. members have said with regard to these estimates being

considered by a committee. It is difficult to connect the auditor general's report of last year with the vote of this year. The auditor general's report gives the details of vote 91 which covers:
River St. Lawrence ship channel dredging: To provide for the maintenance and operation of the government ship channel fleet and the government shipyard while engaged in the ordinary maintenance of the existing ship channel, including all necessary repairs and reconditioning.
The amount of the vote was $438,400, of which $394,488.29 was spent, leaving $43,911.71 not used. It is difficult for anyone to connect those particulars with the present vote. I should like to know how much of this vote is really a revote.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon. friend
is confused. In the days when we owned the shipyard at Sorel, and had a fleet, we had an item in the estimates to cover the cost of maintenance. The shipyard was sold some two years ago, and 1 assume the details in the auditor general's report cover the last year the shipyard was operated, probably 1937.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
This is for the year
ended March 31, 1938.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: We had no such item in the estimates for 1939.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
