maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: To what point has the dredging actually reached now? My recollection is that when the minister took over the department the thirty-five foot channel was completed to a point just east of the most easternmost pier of the harbour, and was then approaching the area of the harbour itself into which the piers protrude. Has the deepening of the harbour proper, and consequently of the berths within the piers, been started?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Yes, the principal berths of the harbour have been deepened to thirty-five feet, and the channel of the harbour has largely been dredged to that depth. There are areas of the harbour in which deepening is still in process. The work this year is in the vicinity of the southern pier, grain elevator No. 3. The harbour work is well advanced. My hon. friend is mistaken in saying that two years ago the channel itself had been deepened to thirty-five feet.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Four years ago, in 1935.
Mr. HOW'E: The channel to-day is about 31i feet of usable depth. The work has never been brought to a point where there is a 
depth of thirty-five feet for any considerable portion, based on the 1935 data. WTe have never had a thirty-five foot channel to the entrance of the harbour at Montreal, but work has been proceeding on the areas which require improving. A large portion of work was undertaken last year in the vicinity oi Three Rivers. We have been working on two bars below Quebec, and that work has been completed. The work in the vicinity of Three Rivers has also been completed. The main contract this year will be for work round Sorel island, widening and deepening the cut there.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Is the cut through rock?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: No, it is clay.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Where is the western end of the thirty-five foot channel that starts in the gulf of the St. Lawrence? How far up is that thirty-five foot channel now?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I would say to about the foot of lake St. Peter. I think the work opposite Three Rivers is practically completed. If so, we have a thirty-five foot channel to the foot of lake St. Peter.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Would the minister explain the kind of contract under which this work is now being done?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: It is a unit price contract, covering various classifications of material and specifying various localities. Unit prices are slightly lower now than at any previous time since the contract was signed in 1930. The contract was revised in 1935, and previously it had been extended twice, retaining the original unit prices. There is a long list of unit prices applying to various localities. The contract has been brought down in the house at least twice, but I shall be glad to bring it down again if my hon. friend cares to see it.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: What kind of supervision does the government exercise over the work for which unit prices are paid?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The government has a ship channel branch, for which there is a vote in the estimates. We have a considerable fleet of boats engaged in inspection and an expert staff whose duty it is to supervise all dredging work on the St. Lawrence.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Are these contracts given on a mileage basis or by the yard?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I do not think dredging is done by the mile; it is usually by the yard.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I mean, can the contractor do as much work as he likes within the year, or is he limited to doing a certain job?

Supply-Transport-M arine

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The contract as originally
awarded covered certain areas of the St. Lawrence and a certain maximum yardage. That contract was extended in 1932, and again at the end of 1934 or early in 1935. It was further extended by this government in 1936. To-day the work covers what is required to complete the channel in accordance with the interdepartmental report. The units are yards of material removed, and the prices are as set out in the contract. The work is the work recommended by the report of the engineers, which goes into a great deal of detail as to the areas to be dredged, and the only changes made are slight modifications which a detailed study of the work indicates to our engineers to be desirable.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Then the only limit is
the contractors' capacity to do the work? There is, in the contract, no limit as to yardage? The contractor can just go ahead, and the more he can do during the season, the more he gets paid; is that it?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Each extension of the contract sets a definite limit on the yardage. The limit which the contractor can do in any season is set by the vote we are now considering. When that is used up, we take our inspectors off and say: "We are through; tie up the dredges." The contract covers more than one season's work, and we let the contractor proceed in any one season until we have used up the amount appropriated for that particular year.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I understand that the price for dredging rock is higher than for other types of material. Is that correct?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Yes, the rock price is in the vicinity of five dollars, while certain classes of material are excavated for as low as sixteen cents a cubic yard.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
How does the government
supervise the work in order to determine the exact quantity of rock, sand, clay or other material removed, because the prices vary with the materials excavated? How close a supervision is exercised by the government, or does the government rely mainly on the contractor?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
We have a very considerable St. Lawrence ship channel staff, amounting in the summer to perhaps forty or fifty men, some of whom are highly trained engineers. We have men on the dredges to check the material; the yardage is also checked, and the bottom measured before and after. We have crews of men constantly checking up before and after the dredging is done. The work is done
as scientifically as the engineering profession have been able to devise for that class of work, and I believe their work is very accurate indeed.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: It is not the material actually taken out that is measured and paid for, but what the engineers determine should be taken out at a given point. Is that it?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: We measure the amount of material before the dredging starts, and measure also the amount of material removed. That is called place measurement. We measure the prism of material that has been excavated. Of course the yardage in place is less than the yardage that has been taken up and put in the scow.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I understand that there is a government inspector on each dredge; that a great deal depends upon his honesty and integrity; that he in the final analysis is the judge as to what amount of rock is excavated and what amount of clay is excavated, and that upon his report the contractors' price is established. My information may be incorrect, but I am trying to find out whether it is correct or not, because if iwe are so dependent upon an inspector appointed by the government, a political appointee-I have not in mind this government in particular; he might be appointed by any government-it is rather a dangerous procedure to spend such a heavy amount of money upon the recommendation or the voucher of an inspector who, in the first instance, was not particularly well qualified, perhaps, for the position, but just happened to be placed there by the government which was then in power. I am concerned to find out whether the check-up was close enough, or whether the contractor was able to get prices for rock and clay excavated from the ship channel in quantities which were probably not as great as those recommended in the voucher.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friend is entirely mistaken, first, as to how the work is measured, and, second, as to how the contract is paid. It is true that we have an inspector on the dredge. He is there to report any interiuptions of the work, any movements of the dredge, and also as to any change in material, although the latter seldom happens. A totally different class of equipment is required for working in rock from what is used for working, for instance, in sand or clay.
The inspector on the dredge is not the man who determines the classification. The classification is agreed upon by our engineering staff and by the contractors for the various localities, depending upon the bearings made
Supply-Transport-M arine

by our own staff and upon our own check-up. So far as measurements are concerned, they are place measurements. If anybody doubts the correctness of a measurement he can go back months afterwards and re-check it. It is taken toy determining by actual measurement the level to which the dredging has been brought, compared with the original levels before the dredging was undertaken. These are checked and re-checked. If my hon. friend would care to visits the offices of the ship channel staff I am sure they would show him the checks which are made of that class of work. I might add that I have had to do with work of this kind for a great many years, and I have never seen a more complete set of records or a more complete check than is carried on by our ship channel staff.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I understood the minister to say that when this job of making the thirty-ifive foot channel was first undertaken, the estimated cost was $11,500,000.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: No. The work of improving the St. Lawrence channel has 'been going on for a great many years. In 1932 the late government instituted an investigation fay departmental engineers, experts in this type of work, to recommend a program for the completion of the St. Lawrence ship channel as far as developing the thirty-five foot channel is concerned. That committee studied the subject for three years. They went into elaborate studies of the hydraulics of the channel and the amount of dredging required; they took a great many bearings, and investigated the channel most thoroughly. The report, which I believe was brought down in 1936, advised that an expenditure of $11,500,000 in the manner definitely recommended by the report would complete the St. Lawrence ship channel; that is, from the point of contracts then outstanding. There was at that time some work contracted for and not completed, but the report of the engineers recommended a further expenditure of $11,500,000, and that is the contract under which dredging is being carried on to-day.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
If this expenditure of
$3,000,000 per annum has been going on since 1936, and the minister expects that the work will be completed in 1943 at an expenditure each year of $3,000,000. the total will be very much more than $11,500,000.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The agreement covering this
work was not signed until 1937, and at that time there was certain unexpired work which had been contracted for in 1934. The sum of $11,500,000 was the expenditure required after

the work then contracted for had been completed. I believe this is the second year that we have been working on this contract, but the first year was practically all taken up with work on the contract previously entered into.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
A minute or so ago the
minister made the statement that it cost from sixteen cents to five dollars a cubic yard to take out clay and stone. Is there any solid rock at all at the bottom of the St. Lawrence at the present time? Are the contractors dredging solid rock, or what is there in the bed of the river?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Dredging is done considerably below solid rock; for instance, in the harbour of Montreal at least six or seven feet of solid rock excavation is required to get down to the depth prescribed. Beyond Quebec we struck a bar of solid rock, and that is being excavated at thirty-five feet below low tide, which means some forty-three or forty-four feet below high tide.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Is it not the duty of
inspectors to measure the quantity of cubic yards of earth that are on the dredge which takes the material away.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: No.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Then how is the number of yards that are taken out of the bottom of the river arrived at? The material must be measured after it is taken out. Of course it could be measured up in the first place, but I should think it would be difficult to measure it up at the bottom of the water.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Place measurement is much
more accurate than scow measurement.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
At the bottom of the
river?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Certainly. That is where
we measure it.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Engineers must have good
imaginations. I have been mixed up in a good deal of that kind of work.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
How many miles of this
ship channel have been completed and how many remain to be excavated. I should also like to know whether, after certain portions have been completed, they fill in through the action of the current and so on as time goes by, so that more work is required.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I do not know just where the channel may be said to start. It begins well below Quebec, that is where bars have been taken out, but I do not know how far down the gulf one would say that the channel

Supply-Transport-Marine
starts. It has been completed up to the foot of lake Saint Peter, which is a little above Three Rivers. That part has been completed to thirty-five feet. Three Rivers is, I suppose, about sixty-two miles below Montreal, so that we are working to-day in the sixty-two miles of channel between Three Rivers and Montreal. If the hon. member knows the St. Lawrence river, he knows that there are deep parts and shallow parts. It is not as though one went out on the prairie and dug a trench. I have forgotten the other question.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Does the channel silt up?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
No. Fortunately there is
very little silting in the St. Lawrence. The committee will notice that a little further on we have a small maintenance vote. I believe that maintenance costs about $200,000 a year, which is very little for a channel of that length.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: What is the estimated cost of the final completion, over a period of years, of the channel?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Well, it is $11,500,000, less
the work we have done under this contract. I cannot say how much of the work done in the last three years was under this contract or under the contract which was let previously, but I should say the cost still to be met is about seven or eight million dollars.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Including the present contract, what is the total amount that has been expended on developing the ship channel to a prospective depth of thirty-five feet in order to make Montreal harbour available at that depth?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The total expenditure to
March 1, 1938, for dredging, plant, shops, surveys, et cetera, was $73,087,695.31.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Then we have to add the balance of the present contract to that, whatever the balance may be?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: So that the total expenditure on that ship channel so far will be over $80,000,000?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: That is to complete it. .

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Does not the continual dredging and deepening of the channel progressively lower the water? Does the minister contemplate the construction of weirs to take the place of this continual dredging? The dredging lowers the water so that it will become necessary to put in weirs to maintain the water at a desired level.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The report of the engineers, to which I have already referred, went into that matter fully. There have been suggestions that the water be raised by a series of dams and locks and that an attempt be made through weirs to raise the level and thus avoid dredging. The report in question was of the opinion that no further remedial works were necessary and that the dredging required to complete the channel would not lower the water level in the harbour of Montreal sufficiently to warrant further compensation. There are a number of weirs already in the St. Lawrence and they are being maintained. We have a vote this year to repair some scouring on the weirs to top them out, and that work will be carried out.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Two years ago the minister took a drastic step when he disposed of the equipment at Sorel which belonged formerly to the government. I did not know at the time whether the move was a wise one but we readily accepted the minister's assurances inasmuch as he was an engineer and more or less an expert in matters of this sort. He thought the deal was a good one as far as the government was concerned. The matter has caused a good deal of feeling among the people of Sorel because I get letters from them still bemoaning the fact that the government no longer owns the plant and equipment. It is about two years since they were disposed of. Will the minister now give the committee his opinion on the question as to what advantages have accrued to the government from the sale of the plant and equipment? Is it now used by the company who have the contract for dredging in the St. Lawrence?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: No one connected with the department has any doubt that the dredging is carried on with vastly greater efficiency now than previously.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: More economically?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Yes. We are satisfied that we get a greater yardage for the same expenditure than we obtained when we took out a part with our own fleet. In disposing of the shipyard we disposed of an operating problem that had been a nightmare to the department for many years, and we are of the opinion that no great hardship has been caused the citizens of' Sorel because the work is still done from that point by private contractors. The men formerly engaged in our work now work for private contractors. Perhaps they are required to work a little harder, but that is not very serious. In any event there is no question that the efficiency of the work has been greatly improved. We also
Supply-Transport-M arine

had to face the fact that with the completion of the channel, which is now only a few years distant, that plant would be a drug on the market. I am sure we did well to dispose of it at what proved to be the peak of the market for that class of equipment.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Is the same class of equipment now used for dredging the channel?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Very little. There are two or three dredges being used, but the work performed by the old government fleet is less than 20 per cent of the total work done by the contractors.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: In view of the fact that it is unnecessary to do any dredging whatsoever in certain ports where national harbour boards operate-and I have in mind particularly the port of Halifax-may I ask whether any part of these millions of dollars is chargeable against the operations of the national harbours board, or whether any interest is chargeable to the operations of the national harbours board controlling the St. Lawrence.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I think that is in the same position as capital in the port of Halifax. We can charge it all we like, but we cannot collect interest on it. It is not charged directly to the port of Halifax.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The point is this. The overhead, I understand, takes account of the operations of each of these ports. Separate statements are now required, and it is only fair that if there is a charge running into millions against certain ports, for their development, a proportion of that expenditure should be assessed directly to each of the particular ports affected. On the one hand, we have between $73,000,000 and $80,000,000 spent on dredging to assist the shipping of three ports on the St. Lawrence, and on the other we find practically not a dollar spent on dredging in the harbour of Halifax; nevertheless those using that port have to pay dockage charges and harbour dues, on the same scale 'as those who use other ports where millions of dollars have been spent to improve them and make it possible for them to carry on their business.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The development of the St. Lawrence is not a matter of developing individual harbours. It is the development of a great inland waterway which goes from the sea to the head of the great lakes and serves a very considerable part of Canada and the United States. It is regarded, and quite properly so, as work for the benefit of all Canada. Expenditures for harbour improvements in

any of the harbours of the St. Lawrence, are, of course, capitalized for the harbour, just as they are in ports and in the maritimes and on the Pacific. But as regards the inland waterway, it is charged to the country as a whole.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: This is a very large item inasmuch as it involves an expenditure of over $3,250,000, and I find in the special supplementary estimates further sums of $400,000 and $200,000 provided for exactly the same type of work. In addition, this is only a portion of a very large contract which altogether may amount to some $11,500,000. A great deal more information should be given to the committee before an item of this kind should pass. For example, I believe it would be in the interest of all concerned if the minister would tell us what company purchased the equipment which formerly was owned by the government at Sorel.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend gave the committee a great deal of information on that subject last year, and I gave my hon. friend a great deal of information, including that for which he has just asked. Does he want me to carry on that discussion again?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I cannot see the point. Here is an item before us involving some $3,250,000, and apparently the minister does not think it of sufficient importance to warrant giving information to the committee. It is a large sum, and I think we are entitled to the information. I should like to know who purchased this equipment.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: If the hon. member will look at his notes of last year it will be obvious to him.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: That is not the answer I should like to get. I think the committee would like to have the information. I wish to know what company purchased this equipment.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Look at last year's
Hansard.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I do not intend to look at last year's Hansard. The minister has plenty of time, so have we. Here is an item of $3,250,000 plus $600,000 in the supplement-aries, and we are refused information about it. The minister says we got the information last year, but I am under the impression that there has been a change in the name of the company since the contract was signed. I should like the minister to tell us the name of the company which purchased this equipment at Sorel, that formerly belonged to the government.

Supply-Trcimport-M arine

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: If it will help my hon. friend I may say this company is Marine Industries Limited, formerly General Dredging Contractors Limited.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: How much money has been paid by Marine Industries Limited on account of the goods purchased from the government by them?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Every payment has been
made on its exact due date. I cannot give the amount offhand.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: That does not answer the question. I did not ask the date of payment. I asked how much money has been paid.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I have not that information.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: If the minister expects the committee to pass an amount of $3,250,000 which will be paid to this company that got the equipment by purchase from the government, he should be prepared to answer questions. I believe it is part of the contract that the company which purchased this equipment from the government are not paying for the equipment until they receive some money out of the contract which they have * been given by the government. I should like the minister to inform the committee on that point.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend did his muckraking on this subject last year. I do not know that I care to take very much more of it.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: He made all sorts of statements accusing me of dishonesty. I went into the subject fully last year. I do not know why I should have to do so again.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I rise to a point of
order.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Sit down.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I will not sit down.
I am speaking to a point of order.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I am on my feet at the
moment.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I did not accuse the minister of dishonesty at any time, as the minister well knows, and I think he should withdraw that statement.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member certainly
did accuse me of dishonesty.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I should like to have a ruling on that point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: What is the point of order?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The point of order is that the minister states that I accused him of dishonesty. I did no such thing and I should like him to withdraw that statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I did not hear the minister make any statement charging the hon. member with dishonesty.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Well, I am bound to abide by your ruling, but I am inclined to think that the muckraking is at the bottom of the St. Lawrence river and not in this committee. However, if the minister does not want to give that information, perhaps there is other information he can supply. I realize that the sale of this equipment was undertaken on the recommendation of a certain engineer of the department. I notice that the chief engineer who recommended the sale is a gentleman named J. E. St. Laurent. I should like to know how long he had been appointed before he made that recommendation to the government.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: To my knowledge, Mr. J. E. St. Laurent has been in the service of the federal government for more than thirty years. He was transferred when we lost two senior engineers, one by retirement and the other by sudden death. Mr. St. Laurent was then placed in charge of that work. I think he had been there for some eight or nine months before he made the report. What is my hon. friend insinuating anyway?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I am not insinuating anything. I think that is unfair.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: We went into the sale of this equipment very fully last year. I do not know that I am prepared to go into it again.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I am not here to defend the minister, but if the hon. member has anything to insinuate let him establish his facts.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I am of the opinion that bringing up this matter, which was discussed very fully last year-I think for hours if my memory is right, and now the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) wants to go into the same debate again-is out of order.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think
the attitude adopted by the minister is unsatisfactory to this committee. It does not make any difference what questions the hon. member for Peace River asked last year, he has not forfeited any right to ask questions this year, and the minister is bound to answer those questions as far as he is able, without regard to what was said last year. I think the minister is doing himself an injustice, and I say this just as much to protect the minister
Supply-Transport-Marine

as to see that the hon. member for Peace River has his rights. The minister should ignore what was said last year. If he feels that what the hon. member for Peace River said was not justified, no blame attaches to the minister about the matter, and to say that because the hon. member for Peace River said certain things last year the minister is not going to answer his questions this year is not good enough for this committee. The minister is unjust not only to the committee but to himself.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
That is enough;
sit down.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I know when I have said enough and I will sit down when I have finished.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: This is a free parliament.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The minister has no more right here than I have or the hon. member for Peace River has, and I am going to exercise my right regardless of what hon. members opposite may say. I have never had anything but the most harmonious relations with the Minister of Transport; I am speaking now just as much in his interest as in that of the hon. member for Peace River, and any fair-minded member of this house, I do not care what side he is on, will take that position. The hon. member for Peace River is entitled to an answer to his question in so far as the minister has the information, without regard to what was said last year.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Let the hon. member for Peace River make his charges here and substantiate them.
. An hon. MEMBER: There is no charge.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The hon. member for Peace River is not, I understand, making a charge. Although the minister may not like the question, he should answer it because, as has been pointed out, this is a free parliament; the minister is responsible to parliament, and members of parliament have a right to this information.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: To what information?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Whatever information is asked for by hon. members.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Let the hon. member make his charge.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I do not know what the hon. member for Peace River is after or is getting at, but he has a right to an answer to his question.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Matters have come to a pretty pass when a member cannot rise in his place in this committee and ask a civil question of the government without being told he is making a charge. I submit that this item has not been discussed yet. It was not discussed last year, because we are now considering an entirely new amount of money which it is proposed to spend this year, and what we have before us now has absolutely nothing to do with the amount of money that was spent last year. I do not understand why the hon. member should say I have a charge to make. All I am asking for is certain information I should like to get-

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: What is it?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I would certainly
appreciate getting the information from the minister. I was referring to the chief engineer on the St. Lawrence waterways; and I wanted to know how long he had been appointed before he recommended to the government that the dredging fleet at Sorel should be sold, and the minister replied that it was seven or eight months. I should like to know if the minister is sure, or if he is stating that from memory.	,

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Will the hon. member give the date of the recommendation which he has before him?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I will give more than that. I will read the letter recommending the sale of the shipyard.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: On a point of order; I see nothing in this item before us which refers to the sale of a shipyard. No part of this appropriation is for that purpose. I should like to know whether or not this discussion is in order. I tabled all the information I had last year, in full-everything the hon. member asked for. I cannot carry this in my mind, from year to year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: On the point of order raised by the Minister of Transport, in my ruling given a few minutes ago I had that same thought in mind, that to bring back the whole debate which went on last year concerning the equipment that was sold, and to bring it up on the item now before the committee, is out of order.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I protest against that ruling.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Sit down, Waterloo!

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Just a minute-

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I rise to a point of order.

Supply-Transport-Marine

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I want the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, who referred to me in that iway, to withdraw.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Will the hon. member for Waterloo South resume his seat?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: What about the other fellow?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I have already made my ruling, and it is not debatable.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I rise to a point of order to draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that the interruptions from the other side of the house are discourteous and undignified in any public institution such as parliament.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Is that so?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: No.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I will leave the matter of the letter, 'because there is other information I should like to have. Have the government now any equipment available 'by the use of which they could undertake to do this work, instead of giving it out by contract work?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: We have no dredging equipment in the ship channel organization. We have certain stone lifters, certain inspection boats, and certain equipment used in maintenance, but we disposed of our dredging fleet.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: If that is so, I should like to know what balance of the contract is yet to be performed in connection with this matter, and if any equipment which was sold by the government is now being used by the contractors doing the work?

sailors in Canada have longer hours of work than sailors in almost any other country that has a considerable marine service. From all the information I have been able to gather, Great Britain and the United States have an eight-hour day for sailors. I think it is time not only for us to ratify the Geneva convention which the minister mentioned, and in other years I have asked him several questions in regard to that convention, but we should have legislation putting the eight-hour day into effect for seamen. maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

The Department of Labour has given a great deal of study to the matter; and there, again, the department is somewhat doubtful as to the question of jurisdiction under the British North America Act. I am told that as yet Britain has not ratified that convention. We hope that some progress in the matter of jurisdiction can be made so that there will be an advance towards the eight-hour day, in which, of course, everyone in Canada believes.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

Marine service.
424- Maintenance and repairs to wharves, $7,500.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
On this item I wish to
make another appeal to the minister for some action which will clear away our difficulties with regard to the appointment of wharfingers along the coast of British Columbia. I do so because at a number of points representative committees have made complaints to me and asked that something should be done, and I have endeavoured to lay the matter before the officers of the department and before the minister.
Under the act the minister has the power to avoid any difficulty, because, after all, section 6 provides that the minister may appoint such officers, clerks or labourers as he may think proper. That authority is permissive and not mandatory. But as soon as the wharfinger is appointed, it does become mandatory to collect top wharfage tolls and side wharfage dues. The wharfingers receive on the tolls collected a commission of 50 per cent for amounts up to $200 and 15 per cent for amounts above $200. In the majority of the communities with which I am familiar there is a great protest because the wharf is the only means of access to the outside world, and the people see no reason why they should be penalized by a special tax. They cannot understand why the government should do what is equivalent to erecting a toll-gate across a road. It is as obnoxious as a toll-gate would be.
The minister has advanced the reason that it is necessary to collect revenue. Sessional paper No. 155 shows that revenue is collected only from a comparatively small number of wharves. The wharves and piers in Canada under the control of the department number 1,899, and of these 267 were in British Columbia as at December 31, 1938. Some still remain
under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works, but the wharfingers appointed on such wharves in Canada number 632, there being forty-nine in British Columbia. That is to say, out of 267 wharves in British Columbia, forty-nine have wharfingers and only forty-nine communities pay top wharfage tolls. The residents of these communities pay not only top wharfage tolls but the dues and tolls on goods shipped to them from the port of Vancouver.
The question of revenue does not seem to be as important as formerly. According to the return brought down, the gross collections of top wharfage dues in Canada for 1937-38 amounted to $222,531. The commission to wharfingers amounted to $33,487, and expenses amounted to $14,194. The net collections were, therefore, $174,849. Gross collections in British Columbia amounted to $34,923 and commissions paid were $4,677, expenses being $10,919. Net collections were, therefore, $19,326.
I asked in my question for the returns of side wharfage tolls, because it was brought to my attention that in the case of some wharves where the residents paid top wharfage tolls the steamship companies do not pay side wharfage tolls. I am informed that the Union Steamship Company, whose ships visit the great majority of these points, pay a monthly commutation rate for only a given number of points, and at some points where they do not pay side wharfage tolls the residents pay top wharfage tolls. In the rates set for the carriage of goods to and from these communities many pay twice, because these rates are set to include tolls in and out of the port of Vancouver.
The minister should give consideration to the principle involved. Even though he may desire to collect revenue to reimburse the department for expenditures in connection with administration of wharves, this is an additional tax upon the residents of the communities, over and above the tax they pay for general service facilities, and it is a most serious handicap on them, particularly on producers who bring in hay and feed or in communities that ship out canned or fresh fruits for the outside market. The toll, however small it may be, is a hardship and is certainly a great inconvenience.
I realize that it is difficult to get men to accept the post of wharfinger because very few men of the right calibre are willing to undertake responsibilities that bring them into public disfavour. It is a job which few men want because sentiment runs high against the appointment in many of these communities. If, however, a man is appointed and is
Supply-Transport-Marine

empowered to collect dues from the residents, then it is good business to have businesslike regulations governing the performance of his duties. On that point I have received a great number of complaints in the past year. The wharfinger appointed is usually a man who does other work, and very often the wharf is some distance from the village. He has no regular hours of work at the wharf. He is there during the hours in which the boat docks, and then he goes on to perform his other duties elsewhere. He carries with him the key to the freight shed of the wharf. Shippers in that community come sometimes during the day, if the boat docks in the evening, as it very often does, and they have to search for the wharfinger all over the community before they can get their goods out of the freight shed. In one community it has been the custom to leave the key of the shed at a nearby store, but that offered no protection to the public with regard to their goods, and the practice was discontinued.
In some communities this is a serious inconvenience especially in view of the opening up of logging operations. The logging operators are bringing in gas and oil and are shipping equipment in and out, and it is a great inconvenience when they cannot get their goods readily. If they send a truck driver to pick up goods on the wharf he has to search through the whole community to find the wharfinger before he can get goods unloaded from the boat the previous day. Surely it should be possible to issue instructions to ensure that the wharfinger is on duty during hours that meet the convenience of the public.
I suggest that the minister should institute a careful check upon the manner in which funds are collected in this way. I do not know what the procedure is, but as far as I can ascertain the wharfingers are not required to give receipts, nor does it appear that they retain any duplicates which are open to inspection by the department. I mentioned the other evening that fishermen in distress, tying up at wharves, were charged in two instances the sum of fifty cents. The minister was kind enough to look into the matter. I had intended to secure affidavits when I found that the wharfinger who had violated the regulations in regard to these fishermen had died.
There is no protection in this regard, and we hear rumours, which need to be verified, that some wharfingers levy extortionate charges upon fishermen. Clearly fishermen plying their trade are exempt under the regulations. I would urge that receipts be issued. Motor-car dealers shipping cars in and out of these communities have been unable to obtain

receipts. It may foe only forty or fifty or sixty cents for unloading a car, but the man handling the car for his client is unable to show a receipt. A truck driver or a taxi driver going to receive goods is required to pay a toll on the goods, and he cannot collect from his client because he cannot produce a receipt.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: May I interrupt? It is entirely illegal for a wharfinger to collect any money, no matter how small, without giving a receipt. Is my hon. friend able to give me the names of the wharves where these things happen? After all, he is making serious charges against the whole staff of wharfingers.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I trust the minister does not misunderstand me; I am not making charges.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Well, the hon. member is saying that illegal practices go on, because it is distinctly illegal for any wharfinger to collect any sum without giving a receipt, and the hon. member says it is done frequently. I think it is only fair to the officers of the department that he should name the localities where this occurs.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I am reciting facts brought to my attention.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Does the hon. member think it is fair to pass them on without some verification? He is slandering a large class of people, because we have a great many wharfingers on the Pacific coast.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Well, the complaint was made to me that in some instances the wharfinger was unwilling to give a receipt, and I was unaware of any practice in the department that required the retention of a duplicate receipt.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The wharfinger is required
to make it out in quadruplicate, four copies.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I thought that referred
only to bills of lading. I am glad to have that information from the minister. Other complaints have reached me. For instance, at another wharf the wharfinger is a little autocratic in the performance of his duties, he has assumed power to regulate motor-car traffic on these docks. This happens to be a summer resort with a considerable number of people embarking and disembarking-

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: May I ask the name of that dock?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
This is Roberts Creek. Sometimes in the summer the boat may be tied up at the dock for forty-five minutes, and if the wharfinger decides that he is not going to allow any taxis or motor-cars on that
Supply-Transport-Marine
wharf at that time it puts elderly people and invalids to serious inconvenience. Again I am not making any charge, but definite instructions should be issued so as to safeguard the convenience of the public.
Again, in another community it is reported that the wharf is a mile from the village and the residence of the wharfinger. The freight shed is locked except prior to the arrival of the boat. The shipper has to make out his own bill of lading, and the users of the wharf have felt that no more actual service is rendered now than in the years before the wharfinger was appointed.
In another instance a shipper was shipping a few boxes of apples by the mail boat; he put them in a rowboat and rowed them to the boat; the wharfinger made out the bill of lading, the shipper had to load the fruit on the boat himself, but the wharfinger made out his bill and got his share, getting extra money from his accommodating neighbour. My informant says that if you multiply these instances a number of times you get a large sized grievance. I submit something should be done to remove this penalty from these small communities. The permanent residents at these points are making a struggle, and the general policy is to encourage settlement in these areas to enable people to produce goods and ship them to the markets and thus keep off relief. In some instances the collection of these tolls is just enough to make the difference between success and failure. I hope the predicament of these people in regard to this matter will receive the sympathetic consideration of the minister, particularly because it can be demonstrated that in the great majority of cases very little revenue is secured and no service is rendered to the public in connection with the handling of goods over the wharves.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The department simply carries out the legislation. I was mistaken when I said that the legislation was mandatory that a wharfinger must be appointed. That is not so, because a great many of the docks handle only fish or business that is exempt from wharfage. The branch handling these wharves recommends to the minister that certain wharves have a revenue for which a wharfinger is required, and recommends the appointment of a wharfinger at that place. Where the department makes that recommendation, under the act it is the duty of the minister, as I conceive it, to endeavour to appoint a wharfinger. I believe it is well worth while for any community to have a wharfinger. It is impossible for the department to give proper service to a dock and to keep it in repair unless there is someone looking after 71492-195
it, and it is impossible to do the writing and that sort of thing unless there is some little revenue. The Government Harbours and Piers Act provides that no funds can be spent except funds collected in the operation of the dock. W7e are not able to spend any of the funds of the department in operating any dock under the Government Harbours and Piers Act. Obviously, if there is a warehouse at the dock, someone must look after it or it serves no useful function. We try to appoint wharfingers as well located in respect to the wharf as possible, but of course sometimes a wharf is some distance from the settlement. I think that on the whole our wharfingers take their work seriously, endeavour to give service to their public, and that in the great majority of communities they have overcome the first prejudice which existed against anyone charging for the use of government property and have built up goodwill. I could name many communities in which the wharfinger is highly respected for the work he does.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Do any of these wharves
remain under the public works department, or are they taken over by the Department of Transport as soon as constructed?

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: That is the intention. Sometimes the department carries them for a year or so before they are turned over; they usually wait until there are several and turn them over at one time.

maintopic: REFERENCE OF ITEMS IN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The minister says he knows
wharfingers who have collected, I think he said, or stirred up a considerable amount of goodwill. Well, it is not in the district I represent. I could tell him of a great deal of ill will that has piled up. The village wharfinger is about as popular in some places as Hitler. There may be places where the amount of business justifies placing a wharfinger to give the attention necessary, and in those places I think the minister will find there is no objection, because some service is given. Personally I would rather pay the very small fee required and be able to go down next day and get my freight and find it is there, instead of having to turn up at one or two o'clock in the morning when the boat comes in. But in these small places the people resent bitterly having to pay; they claim that the wharf is their substitute for a road, and that they should not have to pay a toll-gate fee. We know that very large sums, if my memory is right, running into millions, have been spent on the canals in the east, and I do not know that there is any toll collected on them. These people have no roads, this is often their only

Supply-Transport-Marine

means of access. Apart from that, as I have so often, submitted to the minister, the revenue that the dominion government gets out of it after paying the expenses is so utterly out of proportion to the irritation that it generates that it seems a mistake not only from a business but a political point of view.
The charges are very small, so small that you can hardly get any man to take the job. I have again and again received requests from the minister-I remember one day I got nine letters from him asking recommendations as to appointments of wharfingers at various places, and it has been more or less a nightmare to me for the last two years. Where people were willing to do this work, I sent in the names, but it is not a case of political advantage, because most often you cannot get people to take the job as a gift. In many instances, not being able or willing to get one myself, the minister left it to his official who put up a notice of a rather flamboyant kind suggesting that the revenue was substantial. Then he got some wretched man to take the job, and after the man found what his revenue was he promptly threw it up. I wrote a letter the other day to the minister's deputy asking him how many of the appointments made by the minister's official still existed, and there was not one. They would take it on for a week or two, and then throw it up.
Let me give an idea of what is in it for this man who perhaps lived, as my hon. friend says, a quarter of a mile, half a mile or a mile away from the wharf. Bill Jones comes down in the morning after the boat has left, and he wants a barrel of flour, which is 196 pounds and upon which the government wharfage is two cents, of which the wharfinger gets one cent. He gets 50 per cent of all collections up to $200-which is a mere figure of speech, because he never arrives at that amount.
Bill Jones has probably had to go out of his way to get this wharfinger. He takes him down to the wharf. He doesn't feel like having to take him back again. He gets the barrel of flour, and he pays. Then various forms are made out. A wharfinger told me he had to make four copies, which he sent to different officers, and then he gets a cent out of it. He wanders home again, because the man who has come for the flour won't take him home. He is home half an hour, and somebody comes down and wants a case of coal oil, and the same process is repeated-but he gets only half a cent that time.
Can you wonder that the man, under those circumstances, does not take the job? No

man would be bothered with it-and that is part of the trouble. I would not go so far as the hon. member for Vancouver North when he said it made the difference of profit and loss in business, because the wharfage is so small. It is about ten cents a ton.
Many of these places are post offices as well. People come in their launches distances of two, three, five or ten miles and meet the steamer. They get stores at the same time, get the mail and go home. It makes no difference to them whether there is a wharfinger there or not. Then the government says, "Why can you not get that store man and that post office man to act as wharfinger?" But he says, "No, it is my business to get the mail out, so that these people who are waiting for it can get it." Incidentally, he sells them groceries.
Then there is another point; sometimes the situation is even accentuated. It would be difficult perhaps to understand it, but let me give an illustration like this: A steamer- generally the Union Steamship or the Canadian Pacific boat-calls at a wharf of considerable size. They put stuff off there. But there is a float perhaps five miles away at which the steamer does not call, because it cannot call there. A float is available only for small launches. It is a convenience for some channel or some fiord a distance from the main line of the ship's journey. Then, if this thing is in force he would have to pay wharfage at this main wharf, and then again when he took it ashore at the little wharf in his immediate vicinity. He would pay double the wharfage then.
But the main thing is that the government gets nothing from it worth anything. It is annoying to the public having to hunt up this wharfinger who, in nearly every instance, does not live near the wharf, because the wharf is generally set out on a point where there are no houses. The hon. member for Vancouver North said that something should be done, and I suggest the minister would save us an infinity of trouble if he said there would be no wharf collection, unless the revenue were above a certain yearly sum, say three or four hundred dollars. The wharfinger gets only 50 per cent of the first two hundred dollars collected; after that, it is only 15 per cent. You can figure out what 15 per cent of two cents comes to, and you will have a pretty fair idea of what it is-of how he is practically wallowing in luxury after he has been in the job a little while!
I must support the minister and the law to this extent that there are places where

Questions
steamers call where there have been considerable expenditures by the government, and where the wharves are large and costly, and the traffic considerable. There is no doubt about that. None of these wharves lasts more than from five to ten years, and they cost $8,000 to $12,000. It is quite proper that the government should get some revenue. But in connection with these little places, these small floats, which cost about $1,500, and where the revenue is not at all important, I believe the government should be able to draw a line and say, "Unless you can reasonably expect an income of four or five hundred dollars a year, we will not appoint a wharfinger." That would cut out a great deal of trouble to everybody connected with it.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
